rows.title: Agricultural credit - institutional structure, NABARD, Kisan Credit Card, priority sector lending, interest subvention
sub: Group-II M2-A-46: Agricultural finance - institutional structure, NABARD, Kisan Credit Card and priority sector lending

secs.t: Institutional structure of agricultural credit — tiers and FIRSTs

x: PACS operate at the village level and lend directly to farmers; DCCBs operate at the district level and finance PACS; StCBs are state apex institutions; Land Development Banks provide long-term credit.
NABARD’s SHG-Bank Linkage Programme, launched in 1992, is regarded as
the world’s largest microfinance programme
The first land development bank at Jhang was established in 1920, bank nationalisation and the Lead Bank Scheme began in 1969, RRBs were established in 1975, and NABARD was established in 1982.

secs.t: Committees → chairman and outcome

x: NABARD was recommended by CRAFICARD (Committee to Review Arrangements for Institutional Credit for Agriculture and Rural Development, 1979-81) chaired by B. Sivaraman.

The All India Rural Credit Survey was chaired by A.D. Gorwala, the Working Group on Rural Banks by M. Narasimham, CRAFICARD by B. Sivaraman, and the Agricultural Credit Review Committee by A.M. Khusro.

secs.t: NABARD — origin, merged bodies, roles and funds — Origin and ownership

x: NABARD primarily functions as a refinance institution for rural financial institutions rather than lending directly to individual farmers.
NABARD supervises RRBs and cooperative banks and operates the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme, but it does not lend directly to farmers as its primary function.
Commercial banks directly lend through rural branches, NABARD provides refinance and development support, and the cooperative structure descends from StCB to DCCB to PACS.

secs.t: NABARD — origin, merged bodies, roles and funds — Lending and funds

x: RIDF is funded from banks' PSL shortfall deposits.
All four are NABARD funds: LTIF under PMKSY (Rs 1,441 crore), Warehouse Infrastructure Fund (2013-14, Rs 5,000 crore), Food Processing Fund (2014-15, Rs 2,000 crore) and the Micro Irrigation Fund.

secs.t: Kisan Credit Card and interest subvention — features and limits — KCC basics

x: KCCs are issued by commercial banks, cooperative banks, RRBs and small finance banks.
KCC covers crop cultivation, post-harvest and marketing loans, household consumption, maintenance of farm assets and investment credit for allied activities.
KCC interest-subvention benefits were extended to animal husbandry and fisheries from 2019.

secs.t: Kisan Credit Card and interest subvention — features and limits — KCC limits and data

x: KCC loans are collateral-free up to ₹2 lakh and may extend to
₹3 lakh
with a hypothecation tie-up.
The Directions cover loans from 1 January 2027.
The AP Pashu Kisan Credit Card provides collateral-free credit up to ₹1.60 lakh at 7 per cent, with a 3 per cent subvention for timely repayment.

secs.t: Kisan Credit Card and interest subvention — features and limits — Modified Interest Subvention Scheme (MISS)

x: Post-harvest loans are available at 7 per cent for up to six months against negotiable warehouse receipts recognised under WDRA, particularly for small and marginal farmers.
MISS is a Central Sector scheme involving RBI and NABARD; the lending rate is 7 per cent, with a 3 per cent prompt repayment incentive making the effective rate 4 per cent.

secs.t: Priority sector lending — targets, sub-targets and PSLCs

x: Priority sector lending norms apply to commercial banks, RRBs, SFBs, Local Area Banks and primary urban cooperative banks.
PSLCs enable banks to buy certificates representing priority sector lending so that they can meet prescribed targets; they do not eliminate the priority sector framework.
Priority-sector categories include agriculture, MSME, export credit, education, housing, social infrastructure and renewable energy, among others.

secs.t: Data — agricultural credit trends and regional skew

x: Ground Level Credit reached ₹28.69 lakh crore in FY 2024-25 against a target of ₹27.50 lakh crore, achieving 104 per cent of the target.

The South accounts for about 48 per cent of credit against 17 per cent of cropped area; the East and Central regions account for about 8.2 per cent and 13.7 per cent respectively, while around 60 per cent of credit is short-term.

secs.t: AP agricultural credit — tiers, credit plan, tenant credit and State schemes

x: The agricultural target under the AP Annual Credit Plan for 2025–26 was
. ₹2,96,764 crore was the amount disbursed, while ₹2,64,000 crore was the earlier 2024–25 target.
AP ranks first in SHG-Bank Linkage, contributes approximately 36 per cent of national disbursement and records 99.99 per cent recovery.
AP's three-tier structure is APCOB (18 branches) at the apex, 13 DCCBs (436 branches) and 2,024 PACS.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The EAC-PM paper reported the concentration of PSL credit in a small share of districts, criticised reliance on PSLCs and called for a review of the 40 per cent target.
At the 236th SLBC (Sept 2026), the CM pressed banks lagging behind to meet their lending targets.
AP pioneered tenant lending using Crop Cultivator Rights Cards (CCRCs), Joint Liability Groups (JLGs) and Rythu Mithra Groups (RMGs).

rows.title: Agricultural marketing - APMC system, e-NAM, contract farming, model acts, FPOs, warehousing
sub: Group-II M2-A-48: Agricultural marketing in India - APMC system, problems and reforms
Group-II M2-A-49: Agricultural marketing initiatives - e-NAM, FPOs, contract farming and warehousing

secs.t: Pioneers, FIRSTs and terms in agricultural marketing

x: e-Choupal consists of
ITC
’s Internet kiosks linking farmers with markets.
Under this model, neighbouring small farmers pool their holdings and operate them as one large field to obtain scale in inputs and marketing.
Price spread is the consumer price minus the price received by the farmer; it indicates marketing margins and the share of intermediaries.

secs.t: APMC system — State law, notified markets and regulated markets

x: The market system is supervised at the district level by the DATMO, the
District Agricultural Trade and Market Officer
Regulated markets in AP levy a market fee of
1 percent
; AP Agricultural Market Committees collected ₹433.39 crore in 2024-25 and ₹429.77 crore in 2025-26 (to December) from it.
Regulated markets provide open auctions, standard weights, recorded prices and licensed buyers; they do not require sale to unlicensed buyers.

secs.t: Grading and standardisation — AGMARK, laboratories and AGMARKNET

x: AGMARK certification is administered by the
Directorate of Marketing and Inspection
(DMI) under the Ministry of Agriculture.
The proposal seeks to end the dual certification arrangement involving BIS and AGMARK through a single regulatory framework.
AGMARK is issued under the
Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937
. 'Grading and Marketing' is a common misprint used as a trap.

secs.t: Model Acts and contract farming → provisions

x: The Model APLM Act, 2017 proposed warehouses as market yards, a single-point market fee, a unified licence and e-trading.
The 2018 model act keeps contract farming outside the APMC Act, recognises the farmer as the weaker party and covers livestock and services.
Online registration is undertaken by the
Registering and Agreement Recording Committee
(RARC).

secs.t: Farm laws 2020 → provisions and repeal

x: This Act provided the framework for farming agreements between farmers and sponsors, commonly described as contract farming.
The Act removed stock limits on cereals, pulses, oilseeds, edible oils, onion and potato.
Trade in the specified trade area was outside APMC yards and without State market fee; the Act did not mention MSP.

secs.t: e-NAM — launch, State reforms, advantages and coverage — Basics

x: The
Small Farmers' Agribusiness Consortium
(SFAC) is the lead implementing agency for e-NAM.
E-NAM is a Central Sector Scheme, not a Centrally Sponsored one.
The Centre provides a one-time grant of up to
₹75 lakh
per mandi for equipment and infrastructure.
e-NAM networks existing APMC mandis into a unified national market under the motto “
One Nation, One Market

secs.t: e-NAM — launch, State reforms, advantages and coverage — State reforms and advantages

x: Exam angle: "which reform is required of states" and statement pairs on e-NAM's advantages.
e-NAM promotes transparent price discovery, brings more buyers, reduces information asymmetry and enables direct payment to farmers’ accounts.
Warehouse trading with electronic negotiable warehouse receipts (e-NWRs) enables produce stored in WDRA warehouses to be sold through e-NAM.

secs.t: e-NAM — launch, State reforms, advantages and coverage — Coverage

x: In March 2026, e-NAM covered 1,656 mandis across 23 States and 4 Union Territories, with 1.80 crore farmers registered.
Andhra Pradesh has 33 e-NAM markets and trades commodities including dry chillies, cotton, turmeric and groundnut.
Online payments were ₹26.88 lakh and only 11 mandis participated in inter-mandi trade in 2024–25.

secs.t: Direct and rural markets → State

x: Rythu Bazar facilitates direct sale by farmers to consumers, thereby avoiding commission agents.
Krishi UDAN facilitates air transport of agricultural produce, especially perishables, helping farmers obtain better prices and higher incomes.
Rythu Bazar is Andhra Pradesh (1999), Uzhavar Sandhai is Tamil Nadu (APPSC 2024 key), Apni Mandi is Punjab, and Hadaspar (Hadapsar) Mandi is in Pune, Maharashtra.

secs.t: FPOs and cooperative marketing bodies → agency and support — 10,000 FPO scheme

x: The scheme provides five years of handholding support through Cluster-Based Business Organisations.
SFAC, NABARD, NCDC and NAFED are named among the implementing agencies.
NCDC
promotes cooperative-sector FPOs, with a target of 1,100 FPOs through Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS).
The scheme aims to strengthen bargaining power, achieve economies of scale and lower costs.

secs.t: FPOs and cooperative marketing bodies → agency and support — Cooperative marketing bodies

x: NAFED is the
apex agricultural cooperative marketing body
and was set up in 1958.
The Price Support Scheme procures
pulses, oilseeds and copra
at MSP.
From 2024-25, procurement under the Price Support Scheme is permitted up to
of production.
AP MARKFED, the apex of cooperative marketing societies, has a ₹3,000 crore Price Stabilisation Fund.

secs.t: Warehousing — Act, WDRA, receipts, CWC and storage

x: e-Kisan Upaj Nidhi, a WDRA digital gateway, was launched on
4 March 2024
CWC was established on 2 March 1957 under the
Agricultural Produce (Development and Warehousing) Corporations Act, 1956
The plan belongs to the Ministry of Cooperation (piloted 2023) and builds godowns and processing units at the PACS level, with NCDC implementing it alongside NABARD, CWC and FCI.

secs.t: Operation Greens and Agriculture Infrastructure Fund → features

x: Tomato, onion and potato are grown seasonally and regionally but are consumed throughout the year, creating price fluctuations.
Operation Greens uses FPOs, agri-logistics, processing and professional management to address price volatility; abolition of all agricultural markets is not an objective stated for the scheme.
Eligible AIF projects include cold stores, custom hiring centres, sorting and grading units, warehouses, processing units and supply chains.

secs.t: Marketing problems → effect

x: Cartels of licensed traders, market and licence fees, commission charges, too few mandis and dependence on approved middlemen are identified problems.
Middlemen and brokers can raise consumer prices and add red tape to the marketing process.
About
of built storage lies idle, which contributes to distress sale by limiting usable storage access.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Haryana introduced Aadhaar biometric verification at mandis before procurement.
Paddy DBT payments in Andhra Pradesh were reported to be made within
48 hours
Operation Greens and PM-AASHA
complement e-NAM as components of the price-realisation toolkit.
NAFED and NCCF
undertook discounted sales during the onion price spike.
The identified concerns include only about 60% of godowns being operational, low digital literacy and logistics gaps.

rows.title: Minimum Support Price - mechanism, CACP, crops covered, procurement, criticism; PM-AASHA
sub: Group-II M2-A-50: Agricultural pricing and policy - MSP, CACP and the price policy debate

secs.t: Indian agriculture — development phases and crop types

x: HYV wheat and rice marked the Green Revolution phase; PDS distribution at issue price marked the price-support and procurement phase; and PM-KISAN belongs to the post-1991 reform phase.
The Pre-Green Revolution phase began in 1950, APC and FCI were set up in 1965, the Wheat Revolution stamp was released in July 1968, and India became a WTO member in 1995.

secs.t: MSP and CACP — concept, recommending and approving bodies

x: Exam angle: "recommending vs approving body" (CACP vs CCEA) is the favourite trap.
The CACP recommends MSP, while the
Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs
approves it.
MSP is announced before sowing and protects farmers from price crashes.
When the market price falls below MSP, government agencies procure the stock offered, providing a safeguard against distress sales.

secs.t: Terms → meaning — cost concepts and sugarcane prices

x: Exam angle: "MSP = 1.5 × C2" is the trap; the actual formula is 1.5 × A2+FL.
A2+FL
consists of A2 paid-out costs plus the imputed value of family labour.
The FRP for sugar season 2026–27, covering October to September, was raised by
₹10 per quintal
FRP replaced the Statutory Minimum Price from the sugar season

secs.t: Crops covered — 22 mandated crops, Niger and cotton

x: Niger seed has an MSP, is a Kharif crop and its oil is used for cooking by some tribal people.
The stated split is 14 kharif crops, 6 rabi crops and 2 commercial crops, totalling 22 mandated crops.
The seven cereals are
paddy, wheat, maize, jowar, bajra, ragi and barley

secs.t: Data — MSP rates, Kharif 2026-27 and the paddy trend

x: The common paddy MSP for Kharif 2016–17 was
₹1,470 per quintal
Common paddy was fixed at ₹2,441, Grade A at ₹2,461, and the common variety received a ₹72 increase.
Sunflower
recorded the largest hike, increasing by ₹622 per quintal.

secs.t: Procurement — agencies, open-ended vs limited crops, wheat RMS 2026-27

x: FCI and State agencies procure all wheat and paddy that meets specifications at MSP, making procurement effectively open-ended.
State agencies procure coarse grains for the Central Pool, but prior approval of the Government of India is required.
More than 35 million tonnes of wheat were procured during RMS 2026–27, exceeding the 34.5 million tonne target.

secs.t: PM-AASHA — components, outlay and performance — Basics

x: PM-AASHA was launched in
September 2018
by the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare.
PM-AASHA seeks to make MSP reach farmers, including small and marginal farmers.
The outlay for the Fifteenth Finance Commission cycle up to 2025-26 is
₹35,000 crore

secs.t: PM-AASHA — components, outlay and performance — Components

x: The Price Deficiency Payment Scheme (
PDPS
) makes a cash payment equal to the gap between MSP and the market price, mainly for oilseeds, without physical purchase.
MIS covers specified perishables not covered under MSP, including
onion
, tomato, apple, chillies, grapes and garlic.
NAFED and NCCF
are the central nodal agencies that procure pulses, oilseeds and copra under PSS at a State's request.

secs.t: PM-AASHA — components, outlay and performance — Performance and pulses mission

x: The pulses mission promises 100% procurement at MSP for four years for
tur, urad and masoor
through NAFED and NCCF under PSS.

secs.t: Price support beyond MSP and in Andhra Pradesh

x: The Price Stabilisation Fund was set up in 2014–15 to hold buffers of onion, potato and pulses and release them to curb sharp price increases.
Potato
is not among the mandated MSP crops and falls under the category of perishables addressed through MIS.
Maize was sold at ₹1,400–1,600 per quintal, well below the MSP of ₹2,400, prompting allegations that the Price Stabilisation Fund had been abandoned.

secs.t: Criticism and the legal-guarantee debate

x: Economists warn that a legal MSP guarantee could distort trade, reinforce monoculture and create WTO-related concerns.

The suggested approaches include wider procurement, price-deficiency payments through PM-AASHA, direct income support through PM-KISAN, decentralised procurement and digital procurement through e-NAM.
The Economic Survey 2025–26 suggested using procurement-efficiency savings to fund
voluntary crop diversification away from water-guzzling rice and wheat

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The central debates concern the appropriate cost base, legal enforceability, WTO constraints, fiscal cost and regional imbalance in procurement.
Kharif 2026–27 MSPs were notified in May 2026, with paddy MSP fixed at ₹2,441 per quintal.
PM-AASHA
(Pradhan Mantri Annadata Aay SanraksHan Abhiyan) is the umbrella price-support scheme whose reach PIB highlighted in August 2026.

rows.title: Public distribution, procurement and buffer-stocking; food subsidy and FCI reform
sub: Group-II M2-A-51: Procurement, issue price and public distribution; food subsidy and FCI reform

secs.t: Food management → objectives, missions and aims

x: All three statements describe PDS objectives: minimum affordable availability for low-income groups, equitable distribution and control of price swings.
The stated objectives are to assure MSP, provide grain for weaker sections under PMGKAY and intervene in markets to moderate prices.
All four statements describe the missions of FCI: procurement at MSP, storage and distribution, maintenance of operational and buffer stocks, and access to foodgrains through TPDS.

secs.t: Institutions → year, Act, headquarters and role

x: FCI is the nodal agency for procuring wheat and paddy under price support, with State agencies functioning alongside it.
Rising operating costs, excess stocks and wastage, and falling issue-price earnings are identified challenges of FCI.
The Indian Grain Storage Management and Research Institute has its headquarters at
Hapur
(UP); Hyderabad and Ludhiana host its field stations.

secs.t: Procurement and storage systems → features

x: Under OMSS(D), FCI sells wheat and rice from the Central Pool at predetermined prices to moderate market prices.

Decentralised Procurement (DCP) began in 1997: designated States procure, store and distribute grain for TPDS, and the Centre pays the difference between the State's economic cost and the Central Issue Price.
The plan includes silos of 50, 100 and 200 MT, procurement centres, FPS, processing units and custom hiring centres.

secs.t: Price terms → meaning

x: States fix the retail price at Fair Price Shops and perform the operational role in the PDS.
The pooled cost of grain, consisting of MSP plus State bonuses, is about
two-thirds
of the economic cost.
A hidden subsidy is a cost not shown as subsidy, such as FCI's carrying cost financed by borrowing (e.g.

secs.t: Data — procurement and food subsidy

x: NSSF loans met FCI's funding gap, kept the subsidy off-budget, and the Budget 2021-22 brought it back into the budget.

Total food subsidy was ₹2,72,501.70 crore in 2022-23, ₹2,11,393.85 crore in 2023-24 and ₹1,99,500 crore in 2024-25, a decline. ₹1.4 lakh crore and ₹0.7 lakh crore are roughly the FCI and DCP components of 2023-24, not totals.

secs.t: Schemes and Yojanas → year (PDS evolution)

x: The sequence was PDS, followed by RPDS in June 1992, TPDS in June 1997 and AAY on 25 December 2000.
AAY was launched on 25 December 2000 for the poorest households, with an entitlement of
35 kg
of foodgrain per family per month.
The COVID-era PMGKAY provided 5 kg of foodgrain per month free of cost in addition to the regular NFSA entitlements.

secs.t: Committees → chairman and recommendations

x: The Shanta Kumar High Level Committee estimated PDS leakage at about
46 per cent
based on NSSO 2011–12 data.
The committee proposed that procurement in surplus States such as Punjab, Haryana and Andhra Pradesh be handled by those States, allowing FCI to focus on the
eastern States
Aadhaar-enabled e-PoS devices and ONORC are associated with reducing PDS leakages.

secs.t: PDS reform schemes → period and content

x: SARTHAK-PDS
digitally tracks grain from procurement to the Fair Price Shop and monitors stocks in real time to help prevent leakage.
SARTHAK-PDS is an umbrella scheme covering SMART-PDS, intra-state movement and FPS dealer margins, with AI/ML, blockchain and NLP proposed for monitoring and grievances.
End-to-End Computerisation of TPDS ran Oct 2012 - Mar 2020; SMART-PDS ran Apr 2023 - Mar 2026; SARTHAK-PDS, the umbrella scheme that subsumes SMART-PDS, was approved by CCEA for 2026-2031.

secs.t: One Nation One Ration Card → features and data

x: ONORC permits a migrant to lift the full or partial entitlement at an ePoS-enabled fair price shop after biometric or Aadhaar authentication; the family can draw the balance at the original location.
ONORC has been rolled out in all 36 States and Union Territories, covering approximately 80 crore NFSA beneficiaries.
The mobile application associated with ONORC is named “
Mera Ration

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh PDS → data and schemes

x: AP e-PDS reports 1.44 crore rice cards with 100% Aadhaar seeding, biometric transactions with intra-State portability, and distribution extended to Mid-Day Meal and Anganwadi centres.
Mee Mart is an initiative of the AP Civil Supplies Department with NCCF to modernise FPSs; its first outlet opened at Lalupuram near Guntur.
Mee Mart proposed 1,000 outlets, of which 553 were ready; outlets were to stock over 250 products and be linked to the Digital Rupee (CBDC).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Stocks substantially above norms increase carrying costs because larger quantities have to be stored and maintained.
All three are recognised issues in the PDS debate: rising economic cost, leakage, and the choice between DBT and distribution of grain in kind.
Andhra Pradesh’s e-PDS covers 1.44 crore rice cards, APSES 2024–25 includes the stated measures, and Mee Mart concerns FPS transformation.

rows.title: Malnutrition and food security - indicators, POSHAN Abhiyaan, fortification, PM POSHAN

secs.t: Malnutrition → terms and meaning

x: Stunting denotes low height-for-age, wasting denotes low weight-for-height, and underweight denotes low weight-for-age.
Stunting, measured as low height-for-age, reflects
chronic undernutrition
Undernutrition encompasses protein-energy malnutrition, micronutrient deficiency, stunting, wasting and underweight, whereas overnutrition includes overweight and obesity.
The coexistence of undernutrition and overnutrition in the same population is called the
double burden of malnutrition

secs.t: Data — NFHS-6 vs NFHS-5 and highest-burden States

x: Uttar Pradesh had the highest stunting burden, Bihar the highest wasting burden, and Madhya Pradesh the highest underweight burden.
Goa, Sikkim, Manipur, Himachal Pradesh and Tamil Nadu
were identified as better performers.
Stunting fell from 35.5% to 29.3% (about 17%) and early breastfeeding rose from 41.8% to 50.1%.

secs.t: Causes of malnutrition → factors

x: Poor dietary habits and food insecurity
are identified as the biggest factors contributing to the malnutrition burden.
Malnutrition is multi-causal, and unsafe water and sanitation can lead to disease and nutrient loss; therefore nutrition measures need to be combined with WASH interventions.

secs.t: Nutrition programmes → launch year and ministry

x: The National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme (
NIDDCP
) is administered by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
The idea of the Mid-Day Meal initiative started in
Tamil Nadu
; the national programme was launched on 15 August 1995.
PM POSHAN (renamed from MDM in 2021) is under the
Ministry of Education

secs.t: POSHAN Abhiyaan and Anaemia Mukt Bharat → aims, targets and features

x: POSHAN Abhiyaan aims to achieve a
Suposhit Bharat
through convergence, technology and a Jan Andolan.
POSHAN Abhiyaan targets reductions in stunting, undernutrition or underweight, anaemia and low birth weight.
Weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation, abbreviated
WIFS
, covers adolescents aged 10–19 years under Anaemia Mukt Bharat interventions.
The 9th Rashtriya Poshan Maah (Sep 2026, Varanasi) had the theme '
Hamari Anganwadi Hamari Jimmedari

secs.t: Food fortification → phases and features

x: Phase I in 2021-22 covered ICDS and PM POSHAN, Phase II in 2022-23 added 291 districts under TPDS, and Phase III in 2023-24 covered all districts under TPDS.
Supply continues under PMGKAY/OWS up to
December 2028
The FSSAI fortification logo is represented by the symbol '+F'.
Double-fortified salt is fortified with
iodine and iron

secs.t: AP nutrition schemes → packages

x: The package includes 3 kg rice, 1 kg dal, 500 ml oil and a monthly nutrition kit worth ₹250, along with ragi flour, chikki, jaggery and dates.
Children aged 36–72 months receive
a hot cooked meal, one egg and 100 ml milk
under the plain-area package.
Children aged 6–36 months receive 2.5 kg Balamrutham, 25 eggs and 2.5 litres of milk each month in the plain-area package.

secs.t: AP under Poshan 2.0 and ICDS → data

x: The adolescent-girl programme is implemented in
ASR, Parvathipuram Manyam and YSR Kadapa
, covering 14,942 girls.
AP ICDS (2024-25) has 55,607 AWCs and 257 projects (200 rural, 33 urban, 24 tribal) in 26 districts.
Poshan 2.0 covers
19.13 lakh
children below six years in Andhra Pradesh.
₹99.58 crore
was released for 9,958 Anganwadi Centres.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: NFHS-6 (2026) shows stunting among children under 5 down to
from 35.5% in NFHS-5, a fall of about 17%, though India still faces a double burden of malnutrition.
The cereal-centric nature of the PDS is criticised for not adequately ensuring dietary diversity.
The cited policy debate concerns the ban on HFSS foods within
50 metres
of schools.

rows.title: Allied sectors - horticulture, animal husbandry, dairy, fisheries (PMMSY), agro-processing
sub: Group-II M2-A-54: Allied sectors - horticulture, dairy, poultry and fisheries

secs.t: Revolutions, terms and FIRSTs

x: The horticulture boom during
is known as the Golden Revolution.
NDDB (1965, Anand) launched Operation Flood on the Amul cooperative model.
Operation Flood built a national milk grid, followed the Amul cooperative model and helped India become the world's largest milk producer.
The Sweet Revolution is associated with honey and apiculture.

secs.t: Schemes → year, ministry and aim — Horticulture and livestock

x: MIDH is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme running since
Rashtriya Gokul Mission concerns indigenous bovine breeds; NLM covers productivity and related areas; AHIDF is the infrastructure fund; LHDCP uses prophylactic vaccination.
The Credit Guarantee Scheme for the Livestock Sector was launched by the
Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying
(APPSC-G2 2025).

secs.t: Schemes → year, ministry and aim — Fisheries

x: PMMSY initially covered FY 2020-21 to FY 2024-25, was extended to FY 2025-26, and is administered by the Department of Fisheries.
The
National Fisheries Development Board
(NFDB) handles training and capacity building under PMMSY.
PM-MKSSY, or Matsya Kisan Samridhi Sah-Yojana, is a Central Sector sub-scheme under PMMSY aimed at formalising the fisheries sector and supporting fisheries micro-enterprises.
FIDF supports fisheries and aquaculture infrastructure, particularly
fishing harbours and landing centres

secs.t: Schemes → year, ministry and aim — Apiculture and food processing

x: The National Beekeeping and Honey Mission implements the Sweet Revolution through the
National Bee Board
PM Kisan SAMPADA Yojana is the umbrella scheme of the
Ministry of Food Processing Industries
Mega Food Parks use a cluster approach that links farms to processing facilities and then to markets.
PMFME formalises micro food-processing units under the
One District One Product
(ODOP) approach.

secs.t: Bodies → headquarters and role

x: India is the largest producer of turmeric, and the National Turmeric Board is located at
Nizamabad
MPEDA is headquartered at Kochi.

secs.t: Data — India's output and ranks — Horticulture

x: Horticulture output was 367.72 million tonnes, above foodgrain output of 357.73 million tonnes, contributed about 33% of agricultural GVA and used under 14% of cropped area.

secs.t: Data — India's output and ranks — Livestock

x: Banana
is India's top fruit by production, ahead of mango, apple and grapes.
Livestock GVA was ₹15.06 lakh crore, representing 30.87% of agricultural and allied GVA and 5.5% of total GVA.
India ranks fourth, produces about 10.50 MT, and West Bengal leads with approximately 12.46 per cent.
The current per capita availability of milk is
471 grams per day
; 394 grams is an older figure.

secs.t: Data — India's output and ranks — Fisheries

x: Fisheries
has been the fastest-growing allied sub-sector, recording growth of about 9.08% annually since 2014-15.
Fish production rose by about 103%, from 95.79 lakh tonnes in 2013-14 to approximately
195 lakh tonnes
The APPSC-GS 2025 key used '
around 23%
' as the share of processed food exports for 2024-25, so pick the option offered.

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh → ranks, regions and data — Horticulture

x: The identified activities include banana, oil palm, cashew, coconut and Araku coffee.
Emircha is AP's digital horticulture programme run with
Digital Green
About 32,000 metric tonnes of bananas were exported to the Gulf through eight refrigerated trains from Tadipatri.
The Survey reported 46.43 lakh acres and 406.38 lakh MT, and identified Rayalaseema for development as a Horticulture Hub.

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh → ranks, regions and data — AP ranks

x: Andhra Pradesh is 4th in coconut production.
Andhra Pradesh, India's largest aquaculture and farmed-shrimp (mostly Vannamei) producer, accounts for about 29-30% of the country's fish output.

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh → ranks, regions and data — Places

x: The 10,606 Rythu Seva Kendralu, formerly RBKs, function as
one-stop livestock platforms
AP is the 2nd largest raw silk producer (61,394 MT of cocoons in 2024-25), with its belt around Hindupur (Sri Sathya Sai/Anantapur) and Chittoor.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Andhra Pradesh
leads India in fruit production; it also leads in shrimp, oil palm and eggs.
The five-year review highlighted in September 2026 concerned the
Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana
(PMMSY).
The Chittoor fodder crisis, with a 62% rainfall deficit in June-July 2026, came with
El Niño conditions
, which weaken the monsoon.

rows.title: Indian industry - structure, growth and contribution; IIP; public sector role and performance
sub: Group-II M2-A-55: Industrial development in India - patterns, growth and structural problems
Group-II M2-A-58: Public sector enterprises - role, performance and reform

secs.t: Industrial FIRSTs → year and place (to 1947)

x: The correct sequence is the cotton mill in 1854, the jute mill in 1855, TISCO in 1907, and tariff protection for sugar in 1932.
The jute mills were foreign-dominated, while the cotton mills were predominantly Indian-dominated.
The correct order is Bombay Dyeing (1879), Lakshmi Mills (1910), Raymond (1925), and Grasim (1947).
Munagala Raja's textile unit at Vijayawada
, established in June 1906, was the first of its kind in the Madras Presidency.

secs.t: Growth phases, policies and economists → since 1951

x: The sequence is 1951–65 rapid industrialisation, 1965–80 deceleration, the 1980s recovery and 1991 onward liberalisation.
Premature deindustrialisation occurs when manufacturing's share of output or employment peaks at a lower income level than it did in early industrialisers.
Cheap imports after 1991 contributed to
the closure of many small industrial units
, a feature linked with premature deindustrialisation.

secs.t: Data — industrial structure since 1991

x: After 1991, the services sector gained the most share in GDP.
The decline in manufacturing's nominal GVA share was attributed to relative price changes.
The public sector contributes about
13–14 per cent
of GDP.
Medium- and high-tech manufacturing accounted for 46.3 per cent, industry GVA grew 7.0 per cent in H1 FY26, and manufacturing GVA grew 9.13 per cent in Q2 FY26.

secs.t: Major industries → plants, places and collaboration

x: BHEL is a Maharatna CPSE with a dominant share in heavy electrical equipment, including boilers, turbines and transformers.
China led crude steel production in 2024, about 93 per cent of planned ironmaking was coal-based, and coking coal was the main imported input.
The Second Plan period, 1956–61, saw the establishment of
Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur
with foreign assistance.

RINL (Vizag Steel) was set up with USSR collaboration; its foundation stone was laid on 20 January 1971 and the agreement signed on 12 June 1979 (so 12 June 1979 is the agreement date, not the foundation stone).

secs.t: Issues — structural problems of industry

x: Deficient basic infrastructure
is identified as the main cause of capacity under-utilisation, although weak demand also contributes.
Industrial activity is regionally concentrated in
Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka
, while eastern and central States lag behind.
Directly employed workers fell from 61% to 47% of the factory workforce (2011-2023), and contract workers now make up about 42%.

secs.t: IIP → meaning, compiler, base year and weights — Definition & compilation

x: The IIP use-based groups include primary goods, capital goods, intermediate goods, infrastructure and construction goods, consumer durables and consumer non-durables.
The weights in the new IIP series are derived from the sectoral shares of
Gross Value Added in 2022-23
The tenth IIP revision uses 2022–23 as base year, covers 1,042 products in 463 groups, assigns manufacturing a 76.1% weight, and is compiled by NSO under MoSPI.

secs.t: IIP → meaning, compiler, base year and weights — Weights

x: Primary goods had the highest weight at about 34 per cent, while capital goods had the lowest weight at 8.22 per cent in the 2011-12 series.
In February 2026,
non-core manufacturing and capital goods
outpaced the core sectors.
In FY 2023, the
capital goods and infrastructure/construction goods
indices grew the most (BPSC 2024).

secs.t: Index of Eight Core Industries → compiler, weights and growth data

x: The ICI is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT.
Electricity
carries the highest weight in the revised series, at 30.93 per cent.
The revised series contains nine core industries and their combined weight in the IIP is 32.88 per cent.
In the old series, refinery products had the highest weight at 28.04 per cent, followed by electricity at 19.85 per cent, steel at 17.92 per cent and coal at 10.33 per cent.
The revised methodology counts only raw coal and uses gross steel output.
In the old eight-core series,
fertilisers
had the lowest weight (2.63%).

secs.t: Public sector → role and commanding heights

x: Sindri Fertilizers, Chittaranjan Locomotives, Integral Coach Factory, HMT, ITI and Hindustan Cables formed part of the early public-sector industrial base.
The public sector occupied the commanding heights by entering capital-heavy and long-gestation sectors that private capital was reluctant to undertake.
Bhilai, Rourkela and Bokaro developed as public-sector townships, while Neyveli became associated with NLC and Vizag with RINL-led heavy industry and port development.

secs.t: CPSEs → definition and data

x: A CPSE is a company in which the Central Government or other CPSEs directly hold
or more.
Operating CPSEs number more than 250, their combined net profit exceeds ₹3.43 lakh crore, and they employ about 9–10 lakh people.
PSU dividends grew while disinvestment receipts fell.
The number of Central Public Sector Enterprises increased from 5 at the beginning of the First Plan to 244 by 1990.

secs.t: Institutions, reports and committees → DPE, PESB, MoU

x: The Public Enterprises Survey is presented annually to Parliament, covers CPSEs with over 50 per cent Government of India equity, and excludes departmental undertakings, banks and insurers.
DPE evaluates MoUs, classifies CPSEs into four schedules, grants Ratna status and deals with pay and dispute-related policies.
DPE classification of CPSEs into four schedules is linked to the pay structure of their chief executive officers.

secs.t: Maharatna, Navratna, Miniratna → criteria and companies — Purpose & basis

x: The ratna categories grant high-performing CPSEs
greater financial and operational autonomy
, including the ability to invest, form joint ventures and compete globally with fewer approvals.

secs.t: Maharatna, Navratna, Miniratna → criteria and companies — Criteria & powers

x: Maharatna eligibility requires existing Navratna status, the scheme was introduced in 2009 with first grants in 2010, and investment autonomy extends up to ₹5,000 crore in one project.

Maharatna corresponds to ₹5,000 crore in one project; Navratna to ₹1,000 crore or 15% of net worth; Miniratna-I to ₹500 crore or equal to net worth; and Miniratna-II to ₹300 crore or 50% of net worth.
Miniratna-I requires profits in the last three consecutive years, pre-tax profit of at least ₹30 crore in at least one year and positive net worth.

secs.t: Maharatna, Navratna, Miniratna → criteria and companies — Numbers & company status

x: The
Department of Public Enterprises
grants the ratna status to eligible CPSEs.
As on 1 April 2025, there were 14 Maharatna and 26 Navratna CPSEs.
HAL is a Maharatna CPSE, while Bharat Electronics Limited is a Navratna CPSE; BEL received Navratna status in June 2007.
The Airports Authority of India is a
Miniratna Category-I
enterprise (APPSC-GS 2018).

secs.t: AP industrial profile → investment data and Policy 4.0 targets

x: By December 2024, 10 large and mega industries had been set up in Andhra Pradesh with ₹12,830 crore investment and 11,925 jobs.
The policy targets ₹30 lakh crore investment, 175-plus industrial parks and doubling exports from $20 billion to $40 billion.
AP Industrial Development Policy 4.0 classes projects with investment
above ₹5,001 crore
as Ultra-Mega.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Manufacturing accounts for about 11 per cent of Andhra Pradesh’s GSDP.
The 2026 amendment requires every CPSE to settle MSME invoices on the Trade Receivables Discounting System, or
TReDS
The Budget 2026-27 proposed using REITs to recycle CPSE real-estate assets.

rows.title: MSMEs - definition, contribution, problems, credit guarantee and support schemes
sub: Group-II M2-A-62: MSMEs - definition, role, problems and support schemes

secs.t: MSME definition → evolution and limits — Evolution

x: The major milestones were the ₹5 lakh ceiling in 1950, the 1991 increase, separate 2006 limits, and the composite criterion notified on 1 June 2020.
The original 2006 limit for a small manufacturing enterprise was investment up to ₹5 crore in plant and machinery.
The original service-sector limits were ₹10 lakh for micro, ₹2 crore for small, and ₹5 crore for medium enterprises.

secs.t: MSME definition → evolution and limits — Revised composite criteria (2020)

x: The post-2020 classification uses a composite criterion of investment in plant and machinery or equipment together with annual turnover.

secs.t: MSME definition → evolution and limits — Revised from 1 April 2025 (Budget 2025-26)

x: Exam angle: "small enterprise is defined on the basis of" → investment in P&M/equipment AND annual turnover.
Under the 2020 limits, a
small enterprise
could have investment up to ₹10 crore and turnover up to ₹50 crore.
All three pairs correctly state the revised limits from 1 April 2025: ₹2.5/10 crore for micro, ₹25/100 crore for small, and ₹125/500 crore for medium enterprises.

secs.t: Acts → year and provisions (MSMED Act, 2006)

x: Disputes concerning delayed payments are referred to the Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Council.
The 2026 Amendment Bill provides a National Digital Platform for registration and additional State MSEFCs.
The mandatory procurement share from MSEs is
25 per cent
; it was raised from 20 per cent in 2018.
The sub-targets are
4 per cent from SC/ST-owned MSEs and 3 per cent from women-owned MSEs

secs.t: Committees → year and recommendation (SSI reservation)

x: Reservation began in 1967, peaked at about 873 items in 1984, the Abid Hussain Committee made its recommendations in 1997, and the last 20 items were dereserved in 2015.
Karve relates to village and small industries; Nayak to working-capital credit; Abid Hussain to deregulation and competitiveness; and U.K. Sinha to MSME finance, stressed assets and timely payments.

secs.t: Data — MSME contribution

x: The IYB 2026 estimate places MSME employment at about 28 crore jobs,
second only to agriculture
The 2023–24 LENSD figures are approximately 31 per cent of GDP, 35 per cent of manufacturing output and 45 per cent of exports.
APSES 2024–25 retained the older figures of 8 per cent of GDP and 40 per cent of exports; later estimates supersede them.

secs.t: Role and problems of small industries → features and issues

x: Small industries are labour-intensive, require little capital and help disperse industrial activity to rural and semi-urban areas.
The IPR 1948 identified difficulties relating to raw materials, finance, marketing and technology.
MSMEs act as ancillary units to large industries, reduce regional imbalances and spread ownership of wealth more evenly.
The Samadhaan mechanism addresses delayed payments under the MSMED Act’s
45-day payment rule

secs.t: Institutions → year, Act, headquarters and role

x: State Financial Corporations provide state-level term lending to small industries under the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951.
SIDBI is the implementing agency for PM SVANidhi.
KVIC succeeded the All India Khadi and Village Industries Board, which was established in 1953.
The Ministry of MSME was formed in 2007 by merging the Ministry of Small-Scale Industries with the Ministry of
Agro and Rural Industries

secs.t: Credit guarantee and payment instruments → key facts

x: PMMY or MUDRA provides collateral-free loans up to ₹20 lakh through
Shishu, Kishor, Tarun and Tarun Plus
TReDS platforms are RBI-regulated, discount eligible MSME receivables from corporates, government and PSUs, and include RXIL, M1xchange and Invoicemart.
Budget 2026-27 mandated settlement of all CPSE purchases from MSMEs on TReDS, CGTMSE guarantees for TReDS discounting, a GeM-TReDS link and receivables as asset-backed securities.

secs.t: Schemes → year and features

x: Udyam Registration, introduced in 2020, is free, paperless and based on self-declaration; it is linked with GeM, income tax, GST and TReDS.
ECLGS was a COVID-19 credit-guarantee line for MSMEs, while World Bank-supported RAMP focuses on institutions, market access and credit.
Budget 2026-27 announced a
₹10,000 crore
SME Growth Fund to build 'Champion MSMEs'. ₹2,000 crore is the separate top-up to the Self-Reliant India Fund.

secs.t: AP MSME → policy, base and data

x: The revamped Andhra Pradesh MSME Policy 2026 adds incentives for
women-led MSMEs
Andhra Pradesh has about 20.77 lakh MSMEs, of which manufacturing accounts for 24 per cent, services 48 per cent and trading 28 per cent.
YSR Navodayam was launched in 2019 for one-time restructuring of stressed MSME loans.
AP MSME & Entrepreneur Development Policy 4.0 covers
and was issued through G.O.Ms.No.69 dated 26 October 2024.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: In February 2026 the RBI said MSE loans up to
₹20 lakh
need no collateral; banks may extend this to ₹25 lakh.
Budget 2026-27 gave the Self-Reliant India Fund a
₹2,000 crore
top-up. ₹10,000 crore is the separate SME Growth Fund.
ECLGS is the Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme, which guarantees emergency credit for businesses, mainly MSMEs; version 5.0 came in May 2026.

rows.title: Industrial policy - resolutions of 1948, 1956, 1977, 1980 and the New Industrial Policy 1991
sub: Group-II M2-A-56: Industrial policy in India - 1948, 1956 and 1977 resolutions
Group-II M2-A-57: New Industrial Policy 1991 - features, delicensing and its impact

secs.t: Industrial policies → labels, year and FIRSTs

x: The Industrial Policy Statement, 1973 is associated with the joint sector concept and the core sector list.
The
Industrial Policy Resolution, 1956
is associated with the beginning of the licence-permit-quota raj.
The IPR 1956, built on the Mahalanobis model of heavy and basic industries, formed the basis of the Second Plan.

secs.t: Persons and committees → policy contribution

x: The R. K. Hazari report examined
industrial licensing
and reported that big business houses had cornered licences.
The Industrial Licensing Policy Inquiry Committee was chaired by
Subimal Dutt
The 1991 policy was announced by Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao, with Manmohan Singh as
Finance Minister
The New Industrial Policy was announced on
24 July 1991

secs.t: IPR 1948 → mixed economy and categories

x: The 1948 Resolution defined roles for both the public and private sectors and thereby laid the foundation of a
mixed economy
In the six mixed-sector industries, new units were to be established by the State, while existing private units could continue for ten years, after which the arrangement would be reviewed.
Coal, mineral oils, iron and steel, aircraft, shipbuilding and telephone/telegraph apparatus formed the mixed sector.

secs.t: IPR 1956 → goal, schedules and provisions

x: Exam angle: "Which resolution formed the basis of the Second Plan?" - IPR 1956.
Arms, atomic energy, railways and air transport were government monopolies under Schedule A.
Textiles
were not included among these specified monopolies.
Machine tools
were included in Schedule B. Arms and ammunition and railways were associated with Schedule A, while textiles were among centrally regulated industries under the 1948 policy.

secs.t: Policy statements 1973, 1977, 1980 → features

x: The 1980 policy emphasised technological upgradation, modernisation and export orientation, with export orientation receiving strong emphasis for the first time.
Economic federalism meant providing incentives to backward districts, including tax holidays and cheap credit.
The 1980 policy allowed MRTP firms to expand capacity up to 25% without fresh approval, raised SSI investment limits and regularised excess capacity.

secs.t: NIP 1991 → background and delicensing

x: Licensing was initially abolished except for 18 industries and was later reduced to five industries: alcohol, cigarettes and tobacco, electronic aerospace and defence equipment, industrial explosives, and hazardous chemicals.
Delicensed units were required to file only
an Industrial Entrepreneur Memorandum
(IEM).
The 1991 reforms ended the licence-permit-quota raj by removing industrial licensing, expansion limits, price controls and import-export restrictions.

secs.t: NIP 1991 → public sector reservation and PSU reform

x: The 1991 policy provided autonomy through MoUs, referred sick PSUs to BIFR and initiated disinvestment in 1991–92.
The 1991 policy provided for
20 per cent
disinvestment in selected public sector undertakings.
Chronically sick PSUs were referred to the BIFR, established under SICA, 1985, for possible revival or closure.
SICA was repealed and BIFR was dissolved in 2016; pending cases moved under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.

secs.t: NIP 1991 → MRTP, foreign investment and finance

x: The mandatory convertibility clause concerned financial institutions converting term loans into equity and, as specified, applied only to term loans of less than 10 years.
Automatic approval up to 51 per cent foreign equity applied to a specified list of high-priority, high-investment and high-technology industries.
The present framework follows a negative-list approach, permitting up to 100 per cent FDI through the automatic route in most sectors subject to conditions.

secs.t: Impact and criticism of the 1991 policy → data and debates

x: Cheap imports, particularly from China, increased competitive pressure and caused the closure of many small units.
Increase in consumer choice
was an achievement associated with the post-1991 reforms, not a criticism.
Both statements are true, and removal of MRTP pre-approval directly made mergers and acquisitions easier.
Removal of protection and import competition hurt small units, while reservation for SSI continued after 1991.

secs.t: Institutions and Acts → year (DIPP to DPIIT; enactments)

x: DPIIT’s mandate includes Startups, FDI policy, industrial corridors and IPR matters relating to patents, trademarks, designs and geographical indications, along with Make in India, PLI, PM GatiShakti NMP and ease of doing business.
The correct order is Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951; MRTP Act, 1969; FERA, 1973; and Sick Industrial Companies Act, 1985.

secs.t: AP industrial policies → validity, targets and sector policies

x: The targets include ₹30 lakh crore investment, USD 10 billion FDI and five lakh manufacturing jobs;
USD 100 billion FDI
is not specified.
The suite includes Food Processing, Private Parks and EV 4.0 for 2024-29, and Aerospace and Defence and Space 4.0 for 2025-30.
Propelling sectors are
semiconductors and electronics
, EVs, aerospace-defence, blue economy and green energy.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The licence raj was criticised for encouraging rent-seeking, creating entry barriers and preventing firms from achieving adequate scale.
The reforms shifted the government’s role from direct regulation towards facilitation, forming the basis for today’s FDI framework and competition law.
Substantial repatriation or disinvestment can offset gross inward inflows, resulting in falling net FDI despite high gross FDI.

rows.title: Industrial sickness - meaning, causes, consequences and remedial measures
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I C-61

secs.t: Sick unit → definitions (SICA 1985 and RBI)

x: The original definition included all three conditions: at least seven years of registration, accumulated losses equal to or exceeding net worth, and cash losses in the relevant and preceding years.
The 1993 amendment reduced the minimum registration period from seven to five years and dropped the cash-loss test.
Industrial sickness generally refers to the inability to generate surplus continuously and dependence on repeated infusion of funds.

secs.t: Causes and consequences of sickness → factors and effects

x: Poor working-capital management is an internal finance cause; aggressive competition is an external demand cause; obsolete technology is an internal production cause; and export-import policy changes are external policy causes.
Delayed payments by
large buyers and government departments
create serious cash-flow problems and are a major trigger of sickness among MSMEs.
The public sector absorbed sick private textile and engineering units to protect jobs, but this lowered the returns of public-sector enterprises.

secs.t: Institutions → year and functions (IRBI, BIFR, AAIFR)

x: Exam angle: "BIFR deals with?" - revival of sick industries (not stock markets, loan recovery or SSI promotion).
BIFR was concerned with early detection of industrial sickness, revival of viable units and closure or winding-up of unviable units.
The
Industrial Reconstruction Bank of India
, established in 1971, was set up to rehabilitate sick industrial units.

secs.t: Schemes and funds → purpose (NRF, margin money, RBI measures)

x: The Liberalized Margin Money Scheme, introduced in June 1987, helped reduce sickness in the small-scale sector.
The Fund financed voluntary retirement schemes, retraining and redeployment for workers displaced by restructuring or closure of industrial units.
The present framework uses IBC, 2016 and NCLT for company insolvency matters, while MSME Samadhaan addresses delayed payments to MSMEs.

secs.t: Acts → BIFR failure and the IBC successor

x: The regime was criticised for procedural delays, legal loopholes and an ineffective revival mechanism; rapid resolution was not a reason for its failure.
BIFR ceased on
30 November 2016
SICA corresponds to the earlier regime replaced by IBC, BIFR was succeeded by NCLT, AAIFR by NCLAT, and debtor-in-possession was replaced by creditor-in-control.

secs.t: Committees on industrial sickness → chairman and outcome

x: The Tiwari Committee was associated with SICA, 1985 and BIFR; the Omkar Goswami Committee examined industrial sickness and corporate restructuring; the Kohli Working Group dealt with rehabilitation of sick SSI units; and the Eradi Committee examined insolvency and winding-up, leading to NCLT/NCLAT.
The Tiwari Committee belongs to 1984–85, the Omkar Goswami Committee to 1993, the Kohli Working Group to 1999–2000, and the T.K. Viswanathan-led BLRC to 2015.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The measure required Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) to settle MSME invoices through the Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS), addressing delayed payments, a major cause of MSME sickness.
SICA was criticised for protecting defaulting promoters, BIFR references were often prolonged, and BIFR was dissolved on 1 December 2016 as the last SICA-era forum.

rows.title: Industrial licensing, MRTP to Competition Act; disinvestment and PSE policy
sub: Group-II M2-A-59: Disinvestment - rationale, methods, progress and criticism

secs.t: Acts → chronology of economic regulation (IDRA to IBC)

x: The Competition Act was enacted in 2002 and commenced on 31 March 2003.
The IBC, 2016 replaced the SICA regime, which had been associated with the functioning of BIFR.
FEMA was enacted in 1999, the Competition Act in 2002 and the IBC in 2016.

secs.t: Industrial licensing → IDRA 1951 and delicensing

x: The IDRA, 1951 provided for licensing of industrial units when they were started or expanded and also provided for Development Councils.
The Hazari Report and Dutt Committee found that the licensing system tended to favour large business houses, contributing to the subsequent MRTP framework.
The five remaining categories were alcohol, cigarettes, hazardous chemicals, electronic aerospace and defence equipment, and industrial explosives.

secs.t: MRTP Act, 1969 → purpose, thresholds and replacement

x: The Act was enacted in 1969 and brought into force in 1970; the market-share limit was reduced in 1984 and the asset limit was raised in 1985.
The
Dutt Committee
, formally the Industrial Licensing Policy Inquiry Committee, recommended the MRTP legislation.
The MRTP Commission was replaced by the
Competition Commission of India
(CCI) under the competition-law framework.

secs.t: Competition Act, 2002 and CCI → provisions and cases

x: The CCI was established on 14 October 2003, has a Chairperson and two to six members, functions under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, and the Act was amended in 2007, 2009 and 2023.
In 2025, NCLAT upheld the penalty but set aside the five-year data-sharing ban; the Supreme Court appeal remains pending.

secs.t: LPG terms → meaning (disinvestment, privatisation, monetisation)

x: Liberalisation
refers to removing licences, quotas and controls and changing the State’s role from controller to facilitator.
Globalisation
denotes integration with the world economy and includes measures such as tariff reduction, FDI and the shift from FERA to FEMA.
Asset monetisation enables public asset owners to use new financial structures to unlock value from existing assets without permanently transferring ownership.

secs.t: Committees and bodies → disinvestment

x: The first round of disinvestment took place in 1991–92, involved minority stakes in 31 PSUs and announced a 20 per cent disinvestment limit.
The Rangarajan Committee recommended
disinvestment up to 49 per cent in PSUs reserved for the public sector
Arjun Sengupta
’s 1984 work was associated with PSU autonomy and Memoranda of Understanding, not with the later disinvestment recommendations.

secs.t: Disinvestment → rationale, DIPAM, phases and criticism

x: Strategic sale, Offer for Sale, IPO/FPO and CPSE ETF are disinvestment-related instruments.
Minority sales characterised 1991–98, first strategic sales occurred during 1999–2004, and the period from 2014 onwards accounted for about 70 per cent of cumulative proceeds since 1991.
Disinvestment is justified by poor returns from many PSUs, fiscal pressures, efficiency considerations and market listing.

secs.t: Data — disinvestment proceeds and Budget targets

x: The proceeds are credited to the National Investment Fund, but only the income generated from it is used.
The respective targets were ₹90,000 crore, ₹47,000 crore and ₹80,000 crore.
Since FY24, there has been no separate disinvestment head; it has been merged into Miscellaneous Capital Receipts.
The 2019-20 target was
Rs 1,05,000 crore

secs.t: Strategic sales → company and buyer

x: Strategic disinvestment is not limited to sale of minority shares through an exchange offer.
Modern Food Industries was sold to Hindustan Lever.
REC was acquired by PFC for ₹14,500 crore in 2018–19.
Air India was sold to the
Tata Group

secs.t: PSE restructuring → institutions and New PSE Policy 2021

x: The National Renewal Fund provided a safety net, including VRS support, for workers affected by industrial restructuring.
Atomic energy, space and defence
constitute one of the four strategic-sector groupings under the New PSE Policy, 2021.
The 16th Finance Commission proposed closing 308 inactive State PSUs and privatising DISCOMs, so A is correct.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Union resistance, the risk of private monopolies and the use of proceeds to fill the fiscal deficit are recognised concerns.
The policy emphasis has shifted from selling PSUs towards earning from them, particularly through dividends and asset monetisation, while disinvestment receipts have declined.
After 1991, APIIC’s role in Andhra Pradesh shifted towards that of a
facilitator
for industrial development.

rows.title: Make in India, PLI schemes, National Manufacturing Policy; ease of doing business reforms
sub: Group-II M2-A-60: Ease of Doing Business - reforms, India's performance and remaining bottlenecks
Group-II M2-A-63: Make in India, PLI schemes and manufacturing competitiveness

secs.t: Manufacturing policies → year, targets and design — Manufacturing share targets - National Manufacturing Policy, Make in India

x: The National Manufacturing Policy aimed to raise manufacturing's share to
25 percent
of GDP within a decade.
Make in India sought to make India a manufacturing, design and innovation hub and set a 25 percent manufacturing-share target for 2022.
The stated targets were 12–14 per cent annual manufacturing growth, a rise in the manufacturing share from 16 to 25 per cent, and 100 million additional jobs.

secs.t: Manufacturing policies → year, targets and design — Make in India — targets and status

x: Manufacturing remains around 16.3–17.5 per cent of GVA, below the 25 per cent target, prompting a strategic emphasis on scale, design and global value chains.
The five pillars are Economy, Infrastructure, System, Vibrant Demography and Demand.
The May 2020 package was about Rs 20 lakh crore, equivalent to approximately 10 per cent of GDP.

secs.t: Make in India → launch, nodal body, logo, sectors, pillars

x: New Processes involve single window and e-Biz; New Infrastructure includes corridors and smart cities; New Sectors include selected FDI areas; and New Mindset views government as a facilitator.
Automobiles, defence and aerospace, pharmaceuticals and medical devices, and chemicals are included in the champion-sector list.
Make in India 2.0 covers 27 sectors, comprising 15 manufacturing sectors under DPIIT and 12 services sectors under the Department of Commerce.
Attracting FDI and global firms to establish manufacturing in India is the strategy most typical of Make in India.

secs.t: Incentive schemes → year, outlay, sectors and conditions — PLI scheme

x: The PLI scheme covers 14 sectors, has an outlay of Rs 1.97 lakh crore, and had attracted over Rs 2.0 lakh crore investment and 12.60 lakh jobs by September 2025.
PLI supports sunrise industries, electronics incentives are 4–6 per cent, PLI-Auto has an outlay of ₹25,938 crore, and it requires at least 50 per cent domestic value addition.

secs.t: Incentive schemes → year, outlay, sectors and conditions — PM E-DRIVE

x: PM E-DRIVE's outlay is Rs 10,900 crore; Rs 11,500 crore was FAME-II (2019-24), which it succeeded.
PM E-DRIVE succeeded FAME-II, subsumed EMPS-2024, introduced first-ever support for e-trucks and e-ambulances, and supports e-2W/e-3W up to 31 March 2026.

secs.t: Incentive schemes → year, outlay, sectors and conditions — Electronics schemes

x: ISM is ₹76,000 crore, ISM 2.0 is ₹1,27,500 crore, MPMS is ₹62,500 crore, and the raised ECMS outlay is ₹40,000 crore.
The 3% extra is for design and R&D by Indian brands.

secs.t: Electronics and semiconductors → data, FIRSTs and plant locations — Data — electronics production

x: Domestic production accounts for 99.2% of phones used in India, smartphones were the largest export category in 2025, and electronics output increased from ₹1.90 lakh crore to ₹11.32 lakh crore.
ISM operates under the Digital India Corporation of MeitY and supports fabs, OSAT/ATMP and chip design.
Mobile-phone production value rose from Rs 18,900 crore in 2014-15 to
, at an approximate CAGR of 40 per cent.

secs.t: Electronics and semiconductors → data, FIRSTs and plant locations — Plants → unit → location

x: The first commercial GaN micro-LED display fab is located at Dholera, not Morigaon.
Kaynes Semicon's OSAT is at Sanand, Gujarat, not Dholera.

secs.t: Zones and Acts → NIMZs and SEZ Act, 2005

x: NIMZs are conceived as large integrated industrial townships with zoned land use, clean technology and social infrastructure.
The stated areas of difference between NIMZs and SEZs are size, infrastructure planning, governance, exit policy and fiscal incentives.
Section 10AA provides 100 per cent exemption for the first five years, 50 per cent for the next five years and 50 per cent of ploughed-back profit for another five years.
The proposed DESH framework would drop compulsory positive NFE, permit sales to the Domestic Tariff Area and be WTO-compliant.

secs.t: Reports and rankings → publisher, parameters, India and AP rank — World Bank Doing Business

x: India moved from 142nd in 2014 to 63rd in the Doing Business 2020 report, and the report was discontinued in 2021 because of data irregularities.
The reports were discontinued in 2021 following data irregularities and ethical concerns about World Bank staff influencing rankings.
Per the APPSC-GS 2019 key, the Doing Business rankings mainly guide
foreign investors
on the ease of doing business in a country.

secs.t: Reports and rankings → publisher, parameters, India and AP rank — BRAP — state EoDB ranking

x: BRAP was first released in 2015 by DIPP, now DPIIT, with the World Bank Group.
BRAP covers areas such as single-window systems, labour, construction permits, property registration, inspections and contract enforcement.
The BRAP 2024 reform points were organised around
Simplification, Elimination, Digitisation and Decriminalisation
BRAP 2024 was the seventh edition and contained 435 state-specific reform points.

secs.t: Reports and rankings → publisher, parameters, India and AP rank — NITI Aayog Investment Friendliness Index

x: The NITI Aayog Investment Friendliness Index (July 2026) uses 953 indicators across 8 pillars, places Andhra Pradesh among the Frontrunners (score 45-50), and names Gujarat, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Goa and Odisha as Top Performers.

secs.t: EoDB reforms → area improved; platforms, Acts and bottlenecks — Reforms credited

x: GST, IBC 2016, SPICe+ and online building-plan approvals are correctly matched with the respective areas of improvement.
DILRMP, ULPIN and NGDRS
are associated with registering property.
Faceless assessment, faster electricity connections and land-record reforms were credited reforms.

secs.t: EoDB reforms → area improved; platforms, Acts and bottlenecks — Single window platforms → meaning

x: e-Biz is a Mission Mode Project under NeGP that enables online registration, filing and payment for businesses.
Invest India was established in 2009 as a not-for-profit joint venture involving DIPP, FICCI, CII, NASSCOM and the States, and serves as the national investment promotion agency.
For a first-time Legal Metrology lapse,
an Improvement Notice
is issued before imposing a penalty.

secs.t: EoDB reforms → area improved; platforms, Acts and bottlenecks — Remaining bottlenecks — legal, labour, compliance

x: Contract enforcement and property registration are identified as significant remaining bottlenecks.
The four labour codes and the draft central rules are associated with labour-law consolidation and increasing formalisation.
The Reducing Compliance Burden exercise is associated with the
Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade
(DPIIT).

secs.t: Chronology → year of each manufacturing move and flagship initiative

x: Make in India was launched on 25 September 2014, Digital India on 1 July 2015, Skill India on 15 July 2015 and Startup India on 16 January 2016, so the order is
B, C, D, A
. Digital India precedes Skill India by two weeks, which rules out option B.
Make in India was introduced in 2014, Atmanirbhar Bharat and PLI in 2020, the Semicon India Programme/ISM in 2021, and PM E-DRIVE in 2024.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The stated criticisms include assembly without adequate value addition, concentration of PLI gains in electronics and semiconductors, and failure to meet the 25 per cent of GDP target.
The AP Electronics Manufacturing Policy 4.0 for 2024–29 offers plug-and-play clusters, while semiconductors are identified as one of the state's propelling sectors.
The AP Single Desk Portal cleared 16,458 of 16,783 approvals (99.20%) within the SLA.

rows.title: Start-up India, Stand-up India, innovation and entrepreneurship ecosystem

secs.t: Start-up — definition, criteria and benefits

x: The Action Plan has 19 points, and an entity formed by splitting or reconstructing an existing business is excluded.
The stated criteria are up to 10 years and turnover not above ₹200 crore for a start-up, and up to 20 years and ₹300 crore for a deep-tech start-up.
The framework provides a tax deduction for three consecutive years out of ten, self-certification and fast-track patent facilities.

secs.t: Schemes and funds → launch, ministry, amount and target — Stand-Up India, 2016

x: The scheme provides loans to SC/ST and women entrepreneurs aged 18 or above for greenfield enterprises.
The scheme envisages at least one SC/ST borrower and at least one woman borrower per bank branch.
Stand-Up India (5 April 2016) is run by the Ministry of Finance through scheduled commercial bank branches, and its portal is Standupmitra.

secs.t: Schemes and funds → launch, ministry, amount and target — Government funds for start-ups

x: Venture capital consists of early-stage equity investment with active guidance for high-growth firms.
Crowdfunding
raises small sums from many people through online platforms.
CGSS was introduced in October 2022, uses NCGTC guarantees for collateral-free loans, has a ₹20 crore maximum per borrower and charges a 1% fee for champion sectors.

secs.t: Institutions and programmes → objective and ministry

x: The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (
DPIIT
) is the nodal agency for Startup India recognition.
Udyam Abhilasha is a national entrepreneurship-awareness campaign associated with SIDBI.
AIM 2.0 continues up to March 2028, with ₹2,750 crore and
2,500 new Atal Tinkering Labs
NIDHI is a DST umbrella programme for converting knowledge-based innovations into start-ups.

secs.t: Data — scale of the ecosystem, unicorns and ranks

x: The government count was approximately 125 active unicorns with a combined value of $389 billion.
India ranked fourth with 61 unicorns, down from 64, and was overtaken by the UK with 70.
India is the 3rd-largest ecosystem and recognised start-ups crossed 2.47 lakh (12 Aug 2026).

secs.t: AP start-up ecosystem — rankings, APIS, Ratan Tata Innovation Hub

x: Spark is associated with ideation, Catalyst with 18-week incubation and Velocity Labs is an RTIH programme.
RTIH targets
20,000 start-ups and one lakh jobs
over five years under the ‘One Family, One Entrepreneur’ vision.
The framework promotes competitive federalism by assessing the policies adopted by states and their implementation for start-up development.
The categories include Best Performers, Top Performers, Leaders, Aspiring Leaders and Emerging Start-up Ecosystems.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Start-ups created more than 20 lakh jobs since 2016, about 48 percent have a woman director, and 53 percent are from Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities.
High start-up mortality, thin late-stage capital and bank risk aversion are identified concerns.
Stand-Up India covers loans from ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore, while MUDRA covers micro units up to ₹20 lakh under Tarun Plus.

rows.title: SEZs - policy, performance and criticism; industrial corridors (DMIC, CBIC, AKIC) and NICDC

secs.t: EPZs and free trade zones — terms, places and FIRSTs

x: A free trade zone permits goods to be landed, stored, processed and re-exported without payment of customs duty.
Kandla was India's first Free Trade Zone and was later converted into a
Special Economic Zone
Falta is an Export Processing Zone in West Bengal.
Kandla became Asia’s first Export Processing Zone in 1965.

secs.t: SEZ policy, Acts, rules and committees → year and provision

x: The minimum land requirement for a semiconductor or electronic-component SEZ was reduced from
50 hectares to 10 hectares
The Development of Enterprise and Services Hubs (DESH) Bill was announced in Budget 2022–23 to
replace the SEZ Act
, but it remains pending.
The DESH proposal removes the positive NFE condition and allows DTA sales.

secs.t: SEZ features → developers, approval, FDI, tax

x: SEZs may be established jointly or severally by the Central Government, State Government or any person, including public, private and joint-sector entities.
Most manufacturing activities in SEZs permit 100% FDI under the automatic route.
S.10AA gives 100% exemption for 5 years, then 50% for the next 5 (and 50% of reinvested profit for 5 more).

secs.t: Data — SEZ performance and criticism

x: SEZs received less than 3% of FDI.
Nandigram in West Bengal witnessed violent protests in 2007 against land acquisition for a
chemical-hub SEZ
SEZ exports during 2024–25 were ₹14,63,669 crore, approximately 21% of India’s exports.

secs.t: Industrial corridors → bodies, smart cities, AP nodes, schemes

x: BHAVYA stands for
Bharat Audyogik Vikas Yojana
All four statements correctly describe BHAVYA: its ₹33,660 crore allocation, FY27–FY32 period, 100 parks and implementation structure.
CEZs involve port-proximate industrial clusters and SEZs, 14 were identified, and they were proposed under Sagarmala's port-led industrialisation pillar.
The integration of corridors with Sagarmala is intended to
reduce logistics costs

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Land acquisition, revenue loss, under-used land and WTO-inconsistent export subsidies are identified criticisms.
One criticism is that
export subsidies
associated with SEZs may be inconsistent with WTO obligations.
The 2026 Budget permitted SEZ units to sell in India at concessional tax.
The VCIC 2035 targets are ₹4.20 trillion manufacturing output, 33% women in manufacturing and 24x7 power.

rows.title: Infrastructure - National Infrastructure Pipeline, PM Gati Shakti, National Monetisation Pipeline, logistics policy

secs.t: Pipelines → period, value, sectors (NIP and NMP)

x: The NMP monetises brownfield core infrastructure assets through appropriate instruments while ownership remains with the Government.
The NMP is monitored by the
Cabinet Group on Asset Monetisation
, or CGAM, headed by the Cabinet Secretary.
NMP 2.0 (FY26-FY30, ₹16.72 lakh crore) was prepared by NITI Aayog, and highways/MMLPs/ropeways have the largest share (26%), followed by power 17%, railways 16%, ports 16% and coal 13%.

secs.t: Financing institutions → year, Act and role

x: InvITs are regulated under SEBI regulations of 2014 and
pool operating infrastructure assets
for investment and monetisation.
NHAI funding includes budget support, tolls, Toll-Operate-Transfer and InvITs.
Central capital expenditure rose from ₹5.92 lakh crore in FY22 to ₹11.21 lakh crore in FY26, with ₹12.2 lakh crore provided in Budget 2026-27.

secs.t: PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan → launch, engines, structure

x: PM Gati Shakti is a whole-of-government, GIS-based integrated planning initiative for infrastructure development.
The PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan was launched on
13 October 2021
The portal, containing more than 1,700 data layers, was developed by BISAG-N of Gandhinagar.
The seven engines are Railways, Roads, Ports, Waterways, Airports, Mass Transport and Logistics Infrastructure (APPSC-GS 2024 key).

secs.t: National Logistics Policy 2022 → target, data, platforms, index

x: The target is to bring logistics cost to single digits of GDP by 2030, not below 5%.
ULIP stands for
Unified Logistics Interface Platform
LEADS was started by DPIIT in 2018 and LEADS 2025 has four tiers (exemplars include Tamil Nadu, UP, Mizoram, Delhi).
Logistics cost was about 7.97% of GDP in FY24, down from 8.84% in FY23.

secs.t: Road and port programmes → sector, phase, scale

x: Bharatmala Pariyojana is a road-sector programme focused on national highway corridors and related connectivity.
All four statements correctly describe Bharatmala Phase I, including its 2017 launch, scale, district coverage and corridor components.
Multi-Modal Logistics Parks form a component associated with
Bharatmala Pariyojana
Sagarmala's pillars include port modernisation, port connectivity, port-led industrialisation, coastal community development, and coastal shipping and inland water transport.

secs.t: Railways — data, corridors and targets

x: Electrification rose from 50.91% of routes in March 2019 to
of broad-gauge routes by October 2025.
The National Rail Plan 2030 seeks to raise rail's freight share from 28% to 45% and expand Kavach.
The Eastern Dedicated Freight Corridor is associated with 1,337 km and the World Bank, while the Western DFC is associated with JICA.

secs.t: AP infrastructure — places → ports and airports

x: Bhogapuram airport is being developed by GMR through GVIAL under the PPP-DBFOT model, and its runway is 3,800 metres long.
Orvakal/Kurnool airport was the first airport in South India built entirely by a State, and it was completed in 2021.
