rows.title: Economic reforms of 1991 - background, stabilisation and structural adjustment measures
sub: Group-II M2-A-11: New Economic Reforms 1991 - background, crisis, stabilisation and structural adjustment
Group-II M2-A-12: Liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation - measures and impact on the Indian economy

secs.t: Persons and committees → role, label and area

x: C. Rajagopalachari
coined 'Licence-Permit-Quota Raj' to criticise the control regime that was a long-term cause of the 1991 crisis.
P.V. Narasimha Rao is widely called the father of Indian economic reforms, while Dr. Manmohan Singh is regarded as the architect or pioneer of liberalisation.
Raja Chelliah dealt with tax reforms, C. Rangarajan with PSU disinvestment, R.N. Malhotra with insurance reform and S.S. Tarapore with capital account convertibility.

secs.t: Causes of the 1991 crisis → groundwork, long-term causes and triggers

x: The 1980s saw broad-banding of licences, easier capital-goods imports, a higher MRTP limit and relaxation of FERA.

All four factors contributed to the crisis: the Gulf War increased oil prices, Gulf remittances declined, NRIs withdrew deposits and earlier current account deficits had been financed by foreign borrowing.
The Gulf War, NRI deposit flight and the collapse of the Soviet Union were immediate external or political-economic triggers.

secs.t: Data — balance of payments crisis 1991 indicators

x: Exam angle: the crisis =
high inflation, low forex reserves and a large fiscal deficit
The 1991 crisis was characterised by high inflation, critically low foreign exchange reserves and a large fiscal deficit.
The Centre's gross fiscal deficit was
8.4 per cent of GDP
in 1990-91, compared with 6.1 per cent in 1980-81.

secs.t: Crisis response and reform sequence → measure, date, status

x: The rupee became market-determined in 1993 and the current account became convertible in 1994.
Devaluation makes domestic goods relatively cheaper for foreign buyers and was undertaken to help address the balance of payments crisis.
Devaluation came first in July 1991, followed by industrial delicensing, removal of EXIM scrips and import quotas, and the market-determined exchange rate in 1993.

secs.t: Terms → meaning: stabilisation, structural adjustment, SAPs, LPG — Stabilisation vs structural adjustment

x: Delicensing, tariff reduction and public-sector disinvestment
are structural measures aimed at improving supply-side efficiency and long-term growth.
Stabilisation is linked with the IMF, whereas structural adjustment is linked with the World Bank, particularly the IBRD.
SAPs are IMF and World Bank loan packages designed to reduce fiscal imbalances and promote long-term economic adjustment and growth.

secs.t: Terms → meaning: stabilisation, structural adjustment, SAPs, LPG — LPG → meaning and measures

x: MRTP asset limits were scrapped, interest rates were deregulated, and private banks such as HDFC and ICICI were allowed.
Privatisation
involves enlarging the role of private firms, including through disinvestment and the sale of public-sector enterprises.
Globalisation involves integration with the world economy through multinational-company entry, lower import duties and freer flows of capital and technology.

secs.t: Liberalisation and privatisation measures → content

x: The 1991 Industrial Policy abolished MRTP asset limits, pre-entry restrictions and controls on mergers and expansion.
Delicensing brought freedom in pricing and expansion; MRTP reform removed asset and merger controls; financial reform included interest-rate deregulation; trade reform removed EXIM scrips and quotas.
Dereservation
means reducing the industries reserved for the public sector and opening them to private participation.

secs.t: Trade and exchange reforms → year and institution

x: The reform framework provided an automatic route for investment, allowed NRIs and OCBs up to 100 percent, and permitted FIIs to enter stock markets.
The identified WTO commitments included TRIPS, TRIMS and the Agreement on Agriculture.
Export-led growth came with the 1991 LPG reforms, which moved India from import substitution to export promotion.

secs.t: What was and was not part of the 1991 NEP — fiscal measures

x: The reform approach associated with the Chelliah Committee favoured
lower peak income-tax and corporate-tax rates
along with a wider tax base.
Disinvestment was first used to bridge the fiscal deficit (later for efficiency), and autonomy came through Navratna/Maharatna status.
The 1991 policy permitted up to 100 per cent FDI through the automatic route in
high-priority industries
, subject to the applicable policy framework.

secs.t: Globalisation → meaning, trade, capital flows, sectoral effects

x: Foreign savings through FDI help fill the savings-investment gap; domestic savings are approximately 30 per cent of GDP.
The IT and outsourcing boom generated services exports and helped cushion India's current account deficit.
Tata, Reliance, Infosys and Sun Pharma were cited as Indian companies that went global.
The pattern of growth was criticised for neglecting agriculture and concentrating growth in capital-intensive sectors, which created too few employment opportunities.

secs.t: Changes after 1991 → growth data, direction, sectors reshaped

x: Foreign-exchange reserves rose from about $975 million in 1991 to approximately
$701.4 billion
, providing around 11 months of import cover as stated.
Economic policy shifted from import substitution towards export promotion, supported by lower tariffs and greater openness to foreign investment.
The post-reform approach lowered tariffs, invited foreign direct and portfolio investment, and benefited from IT and services exports as a cushion.
Banking was reshaped through private banks and interest deregulation, whereas agriculture experienced little direct reform.

secs.t: Criticism → jobless growth, agrarian neglect, crony capitalism

x: Crony capitalism is criticised because economic gains become concentrated among large firms with political connections.
The criticism points to lagging public investment in agriculture and the dismantling of food-system supports in parts of the Global South.
Jobless growth means output grew much faster than jobs, so many people, including graduates, ended up in gig work.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Reforms 1.0 refers to liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation in 1991; Reforms 2.0 refers to digital public infrastructure from 2014 onwards; Reforms 3.0 remains a debate.
The Washington Consensus has been criticised in connection with the 1997 and 2008 financial crises.
The appeal sought to conserve foreign exchange by reducing expenditure on fuel, gold and foreign travel.
The post-reform economy is characterised by greater global integration and an expanded role for the private sector.

The Code on Wages includes the Equal Remuneration Act; the Industrial Relations Code includes the Trade Unions Act; the Code on Social Security includes the Employees' Compensation Act; and the OSH Code includes the Factories Act.
The Code on Social Security subsumes laws relating to provident fund, state insurance, maternity benefit, gratuity and employees' compensation.

secs.t: Four Labour Codes → key provisions and expected gains

x: The Code on Wages applies a
50 per cent rule
to allowances for the purposes of provident fund, gratuity and bonus calculations.
The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Central (Amendment) Rules, 2018 extended fixed-term employment to all sectors.
ES 2025-26 expects the Codes to lift formalisation from 60.4% to 75.5% and add 1.25% to GDP by 2029-30.

x: CGST and SGST
are levied on an intrastate supply, whereas IGST applies to interstate supplies and imports.
Article 279A
provides for the GST Council; Article 246A concerns legislative competence and Article 269A concerns IGST.
GST 2.0 was announced on the 79th Independence Day (Aug 2025) with rate rationalisation and a 40% slab for sin and luxury goods.

secs.t: Reforms since 2014 → year and objective; EoDB rank

x: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission and promotes
cooperative and competitive federalism
Strategic disinvestment seeks to unlock PSE value through transfer of ownership to private investors.
The Jan Vishwas Act, 2023 decriminalised minor offences to facilitate compliance and reduce the burden of criminal provisions.
India's World Bank Doing Business rank improved from 142 in 2014 to

secs.t: National Monetisation Pipeline → year, value, model, sector shares

x: NMP uses brownfield, de-risked assets and mechanisms such as OMTs and InvITs; ownership remains with the government and assets are handed back after the lease period.
The approximate shares are roads 27 per cent, railways 25 per cent and power 15 per cent.
The IYB 2026 reference identifies an SPV for monetisation of surplus CPSE land.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The criticism is that ease of living should be placed above ease of doing business.
The Single Desk Portal is linked to the Visakhapatnam–Chennai Industrial Corridor ease-of-doing-business loan.
India improved from 82nd position in 2010 to
57th
position in 2023 on the Market Distortions Performance Index.
GST, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, and trade facilitation were credited with the improvement.

sub: Group-II M2-A-40: Foreign trade - composition and direction of India's exports and imports; trade policy

secs.t: Terms → meaning: trade theory, terms of trade, remedies, exchange rate — Trade terms

x: According to Adam Smith's concept, absolute advantage means producing a good at a lower absolute cost than others.
Ricardo's theory of comparative advantage focuses on specialising in the good with the lower opportunity cost.
An import quota is a quantitative restriction (QR) that caps the amount of a good that can be imported.

secs.t: Terms → meaning: trade theory, terms of trade, remedies, exchange rate — Terms of trade

x: Under the J-curve effect, import bills rise immediately after depreciation, so the trade balance initially worsens; it improves later as quantities adjust.
Devaluation or depreciation makes domestic exports cheaper for foreign buyers and imports more expensive in the domestic market.
The Marshall–Lerner condition is satisfied when the sum of the absolute values of export and import demand price elasticities exceeds one.

secs.t: Data — composition of exports and imports, largest items

x: The shares are petroleum products (14.48%), drug formulations and biologicals (5.52%), pearls and precious stones (3.56%), and electric machinery and equipment (3.29%).
Crude petroleum, gold and petroleum products
together accounted for approximately one-third of India’s imports.
The Economic Survey 2025-26 traced the stagnation in merchandise exports to
petroleum and gems-and-jewellery exports
; non-petroleum, non-gems-and-jewellery goods, which make up 78.7% of merchandise exports, were not the source of the stagnation.

secs.t: Direction of trade → partner, share and balance — Destinations and sources

x: India ran a surplus with the United States and the Netherlands.
Labour-intensive exports shifted from the United States towards the Middle East, Africa, Europe and Asia.

secs.t: Direction of trade → partner, share and balance — China

x: The United States was India’s largest export destination in 2024-25, receiving 19.77 percent of India’s exports.
China
was India’s largest import source in 2024-25, accounting for 15.73 percent of imports.
China became the largest overall trading partner, while the United States remained India’s largest export market.
India’s BRICS trade in FY26 was $417.5 billion, while the trade deficit was $226.1 billion.

secs.t: Data — trade deficit, causes and policy — Size of the deficit

x: In 2024-25, merchandise exports were 437.70 billion US dollars and merchandise imports were 721.20 billion US dollars.
The merchandise trade deficit in FY25 was
$283.5 billion
, representing an increase of 17.6%.
The merchandise trade deficit for FY26 was reported at
$337.3 billion
, with the fourth quarter alone accounting for $83.4 billion.

secs.t: Data — trade deficit, causes and policy — Causes → effect

x: Services performed well and generated a surplus; therefore, lacklustre services performance was not a cause of the widening trade deficit.
The twin deficit hypothesis links a rising fiscal deficit with a rising trade deficit.
The 1991 New Trade Policy shifted from import substitution and quantitative restrictions to a price-based regime, accompanied by a two-step rupee devaluation in July 1991.

secs.t: India in world trade → share and rank

x: The Foreign Trade Policy had set a target of
for India's share in world services exports by 2022.
The services surplus, especially from IT and IT-enabled services, together with remittances, offsets a substantial part of the merchandise deficit.
Services accounted for about
of India's total exports, compared with 39% in 2014.
India's services surplus reached a record
$188.8 billion
in FY25.

secs.t: Policies, zones and bodies → year, target, nodal agency

x: FTP 2023 came into effect on 1 April 2023, has no fixed end date, is reviewed as needed and targets 2 trillion US dollars in exports by 2030.
The Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (
APEDA
) is the nodal agency for Agri Export Zones.
EXIM Bank provides lines of credit, buyer's and seller's credit, project-export finance and SME export windows.
APEDA functions under the Department of Commerce, the Agriculture Export Policy 2018 sought to double agricultural exports, and MPEDA handles marine products.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: India ranked third in the Global South for
trade-partner diversity
according to the stated UNCTAD assessment.
The comparison is explained through India's
Ricardian comparative advantage in services
, alongside a structural merchandise trade deficit.
The stated criticism is that FTAs have widened deficits with ASEAN, Japan and Korea and have suffered from weak utilisation.

An
import quota
sets a ceiling on the quantity of a good that may be imported, so it is a quantitative restriction.

war-risk and logistics costs in West Asia

EOUs, EHTPs and STPs export all their output, may be located anywhere, and receive duty-free inputs suited to their respective activities.
The Budget 2026–27 measures were aimed at using idle SEZ manufacturing capacity affected by global trade conditions.

secs.t: Bodies and facilitation platforms → role

x: Export Promotion Councils and Commodity Boards promote exports in particular sectors and channel Market Access Initiative support.
EXIM Bank (Mumbai) was set up on 1 Jan 1982 under the 1981 Act and gives lines of credit, buyer's/seller's credit and project-export finance.
PM Gati Shakti and the National Logistics Policy aim to reduce export logistics costs and improve trade facilitation.

x: A
mate’s receipt
is the acknowledgement by the ship’s mate that goods have been loaded on board.
A bill of lading is the shipping company’s receipt and also functions as a document of title to the goods.
Rules of origin establish
the national source of a product
and help determine eligibility for free-trade agreement concessions.

x: The West Asia conflict
disrupted cargo movement, following which the Government allowed procedural flexibility in export authorisations.
The matters raised included regulation of fish-meal exports and export incentives for both aquaculture and tobacco.

rows.title: Balance of Payments - structure, current and capital account, convertibility, forex reserves
sub: Group-II M2-A-39: India's Balance of Payments - current and capital accounts, trends and CAD

secs.t: Balance of Payments — definitions, structure, identities and terms — Definition & structure

x: Under BPM6, the IMF distinguishes current, capital and financial accounts.
Remittances are recorded in the current account, under invisibles and specifically private transfers.
Purchase of foreign assets by residents is a capital-account debit.
FDI, FPI, ADRs and external commercial borrowings
are capital or financial account transactions.
Invisibles comprise services, primary income and transfers.

secs.t: Balance of Payments — definitions, structure, identities and terms — Identities & formulas

x: The current-account balance equals exports minus imports of goods and services, plus net primary income and net secondary income.
The Balance of Payments identity is current balance plus capital balance plus financial balance plus errors and omissions equal to zero.
Balance of Trade equals merchandise exports minus merchandise imports and is a part of the current account.
A positive overall balance adds to foreign exchange reserves, whereas a negative overall balance draws them down.

secs.t: Data — current account deficit trend, latest figures and causes — CAD by period

x: India recorded a current account surplus for three consecutive years from 2001-02 to 2003-04.
The surplus was associated with a surge in services exports, not a rise in gold imports.
The CAD peaked at about 4.8% of GDP in FY13, the taper tantrum period.

secs.t: Data — current account deficit trend, latest figures and causes — Latest data

x: The FY24 external-sector recovery came from moderation in merchandise exports accompanied by a sharp fall in imports.
Imported oil and gold, low export competitiveness and the savings-investment gap are structural causes.
The scheme drew $127 billion in NRI deposits, contributing to a $27.7 billion capital-account surplus and a $20.8 billion overall BoP surplus.

secs.t: Data — remittances and services surplus, the current-account cushions

x: The record services surplus of $188.8 billion in FY25 financed about
two-thirds
of the merchandise deficit.
The United States is the largest source of remittances to India, accounting for 27.7%, followed by the UAE, the UK and Singapore.
Remittances are counter-cyclical and do not create a repayment obligation, unlike debt-related flows such as ECBs or certain portfolio liabilities.

secs.t: Capital flows and external vulnerability → causes, shocks, safeguards

x: The reported weakness in the Balance of Payments was compared with India’s 2013 ‘Fragile Five’ phase, amid pressure from higher fuel and fertiliser prices.
Adequate reserves, low short-term debt and reduced dependence on volatile FPI and debt flows strengthen external resilience.
US rate hikes and a strong dollar raise US yields, encouraging hot-money outflows from emerging markets and putting downward pressure on the rupee.
Morgan Stanley described India as one of the ‘
Fragile Five
’ during the 2013 taper tantrum because of external-sector vulnerability.

secs.t: BoP correction → tools, IMF role, committee threshold — Expenditure-switching vs expenditure-reducing

x: A is correct:
devaluation, import tariffs and export incentives
all switch demand from foreign to domestic goods, so they are expenditure-switching measures.
Increasing government spending on domestic projects
can raise demand and imports and is therefore not ordinarily treated as a corrective measure in this context.
A higher import duty makes imported gold less attractive and helps switch demand towards domestic alternatives or away from imports.

secs.t: BoP correction → tools, IMF role, committee threshold — IMF role

x: The
International Monetary Fund
may provide assistance when a country cannot cover its external deficit from its reserves and other available sources.
Stand-By Arrangement and Extended Fund Facility are IMF balance of payments lending windows.
The C. Rangarajan Committee placed a sustainable CAD at approximately
1.6% of GDP
and also recommended a market-determined exchange rate.

secs.t: Convertibility and Acts → year: FERA to FEMA

x: LERMS, introduced in the 1992-93 Budget, used a dual exchange-rate system comprising
40 per cent official rate and 60 per cent market rate
LERMS was introduced in 1992-93, the unified rate was introduced on 1 March 1993, full current account convertibility followed in August 1994, and the second Tarapore Committee was set up in 2006.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The H1 FY26 CAD was 0.8% of GDP, lower than the cited high-deficit peers, while the rupee depreciated by about 6.5% against the dollar.
FCNR(B) and ECB inflows are considered temporary sources of financing.
The CAD was 0.5% of GDP in Q1 FY27, while FCNR(B) inflows helped produce a balance of payments surplus in July 2026.

rows.title: Exchange rate systems and rupee movement; currency internationalisation
sub: Group-II M2-A-42: Foreign exchange reserves, exchange rate management and rupee movement

secs.t: Terms → meaning: quotes, NEER/REER, devaluation vs depreciation — Exchange rate terms

x: Exam angle: "which statement is false" - the swapped definition of a direct quote (foreign units per one domestic unit) is the false one.
Hedging involves covering exchange-rate risk, and a forward contract can fix the exchange rate today for a transaction to be settled in the future.
REER is regarded as the better indicator of competitiveness because it adjusts the nominal effective exchange rate for inflation differentials.

secs.t: Terms → meaning: quotes, NEER/REER, devaluation vs depreciation — NEER and REER

x: NEER is trade-weighted with base 2015-16 = 100.
REER is obtained by adjusting NEER for relative inflation.
A high REER generally indicates an overvalued rupee.

secs.t: Terms → meaning: quotes, NEER/REER, devaluation vs depreciation — Devaluation vs depreciation, appreciation vs revaluation

x: Depreciation and appreciation are market-driven changes under a flexible regime; official changes under a fixed regime are devaluation and revaluation.
So C. Pair 1 is wrong: devaluation is the official lowering (not raising) of a currency's value under a fixed regime; official raising is revaluation.
A rise in the number of rupees required to buy one dollar indicates depreciation of the rupee.

secs.t: Exchange rate regimes → types

x: In a managed float, market forces determine the rate, while the central bank may intervene directly through forex transactions or indirectly through interest rates.
Post-Bretton Woods classifications place currency unions and currency boards under fixed regimes.
Argentina’s arrangement during 1991–January 2002 is cited as an example of a currency board, which belongs to the fixed regime category.

secs.t: India's exchange rate history → year, devaluations, committees, Acts — Phases → event

x: The Bretton Woods system of 1944 established
fixed exchange rates centred on the dollar
and was associated with the IMF and World Bank.
The correct sequence is Bretton Woods in 1944, the Smithsonian Agreement in 1971, the two-step devaluation in July 1991 and unification of dual rates on 1 March 1993.

secs.t: India's exchange rate history → year, devaluations, committees, Acts — Rupee devaluation episodes since independence

x: In September 1949, the rupee was devalued by about
30.5 per cent
alongside the pound sterling.
In June 1966, the rupee was devalued by 57.5 per cent, moving from
₹4.76 to ₹7.50 per US dollar
The restrictive Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 was replaced by the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, which came into force on 1 June 2000.

secs.t: Changes → effects of devaluation, determinants, impossible trinity — Effects of devaluation/depreciation

x: Exam angle: A-R pair "Devaluation improves the balance of trade (A true) because it raises export prices (R false)".
Devaluation makes home-produced goods relatively cheaper for foreigners and imported goods costlier at home, thereby switching expenditure towards domestic production.
Depreciation can generate imported inflation, increase the domestic cost of oil when demand is inelastic, and make repayment of foreign-currency external commercial borrowings costlier.

secs.t: Changes → effects of devaluation, determinants, impossible trinity — Determinants of the exchange rate

x: In the long run, the
inflation differential between countries
is a key exchange-rate anchor under Purchasing Power Parity theory.
The Impossible Trinity states that a country cannot simultaneously maintain a fixed exchange rate, free capital flows and an independent monetary policy.
Sudden capital outflows can cause sharp currency declines, as illustrated by India's 1991 balance of payments crisis and the 2013 Taper Tantrum.

secs.t: Data — rupee movement 2025-26, record lows and drivers

x: The rupee recorded a 5.4% depreciation in FY 2025-26 up to January and was among the most depreciated currencies, along with the yen.
On 19 May 2026, the rupee crossed ₹96.2 per dollar amid Brent crude near $110 and FPI outflows of more than ₹2 lakh crore.
FII equity sales exceeding ₹2 lakh crore contributed to the rupee moving past ₹96 per US dollar.

secs.t: RBI tools → example: managing rupee volatility

x: The RBI restricts domestic banks’ offshore NDF participation and enforces Net Open Position limits to curb speculative pressure and volatility.
Capital-flow easing included relaxation of the ECB all-in-cost ceiling and the Fully Accessible Route (FAR) for Government securities.
A hawkish stance or higher repo rate can attract carry-trade capital by improving the relative return on rupee assets, thereby supporting the currency.
FCNR(B) deposits
brought in $127.23 billion, helped by the RBI bearing the full hedging cost on fresh deposits till 30 Sep 2026.

secs.t: Data — forex reserves: components, size and global rank

x: The four components are Foreign Currency Assets, Gold, Special Drawing Rights and Reserve Tranche Position.
With reserves of $785.71 billion in September 2026, India became the fourth-largest holder after overtaking
Russia
The reported reserves were China $3.85 trillion, Japan $1.21 trillion and Switzerland $1.09 trillion.
Foreign Currency Assets measured in dollar terms include valuation changes in holdings denominated in the euro, pound sterling and Japanese yen.

secs.t: IMF reserve assets and swap arrangements → nature, basket, year

x: SDRs exist as
book-keeping or accounting entries
in the IMF’s records; they are not physical currency or metal.
The SDR basket contains the US dollar, euro, Chinese renminbi, Japanese yen and pound sterling.
The largest general SDR allocation was made in August 2021 and amounted to approximately SDR 456 billion, equivalent to about US$650 billion.
The India–Japan Bilateral Swap Arrangement is a two-way facility involving the exchange of local currencies against US dollars, renewed from 28 February 2026.

secs.t: Rupee internationalisation → framework, terms, symbol, bonds

x: The framework facilitates rupee invoicing and settlement, promotes INR in international trade and seeks to reduce dependence on the dollar.
The INR trade settlement framework introduced by the RBI in July 2022 was built into the
Foreign Trade Policy 2023
SRVAs are maintained by foreign banks with Indian banks in rupees and enable INR trade settlement.
Russia, the UAE and Tanzania are examples of countries involved in INR settlement through Special Rupee Vostro Accounts.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The rupee was reported around
₹95–96 per US dollar
through 2026 amid the West Asia crude shock and foreign portfolio investor selling.
The RBI kept the repo rate at 5.25% for the fourth straight meeting in August 2026, relying on dollar-rupee swaps and the FCNR(B) hedging subsidy rather than a rate hike to support the rupee.

rows.title: India and the WTO - agreements, ministerial conferences, public stockholding, fisheries subsidies, appellate body crisis

secs.t: GATT, Uruguay Round and WTO — origin, basics and FIRSTs

x: The Uruguay Round was the eighth GATT round, launched at Punta del Este in September 1986 and concluded in 1993, with 123 contracting parties.
The Uruguay Round aimed to reduce farm subsidies, open services and cover investment and intellectual property rights.
The Dunkel Draft contained proposals made by Arthur Dunkel, the GATT Director-General and Chair of the Trade Negotiations Committee, for the Uruguay Round agreements.

secs.t: Ministerial Conferences → venue, year, outcome; Doha Round and country groups — Ministerial Conferences

x: MC1 was held at Singapore in 1996, MC2 at Geneva in 1998, MC3 at Seattle in 1999 and MC4 at Doha in 2001.
The Bali Ministerial Conference of 2013 produced the Bali Package, including the Trade Facilitation Agreement and an interim Peace Clause on food stockholding.
MC14 produced no ministerial declaration, the e-commerce moratorium lapsed, and 66 members signed a separate agreement barring duties on digital trade.

secs.t: Ministerial Conferences → venue, year, outcome; Doha Round and country groups — MC14 (Yaounde, 2026) - other outcomes

x: At MC14, India blocked addition of the IFD plurilateral agreement to Annex 4, although it had the backing of 129 of 166 members.
The Doha Round began in 2001, is concerned with agriculture, non-agricultural market access and services, and remains unfinished.
The G-33 is a group of more than 40 developing countries, including India, focusing on food security, the Special Safeguard Mechanism and special products.

secs.t: Terms → meaning: MFN, AoA boxes, de minimis, tariffication, Peace Clause — Trade principles

x: Exam angle: "Amber box subsidies refer to" - trade-distorting support.
The SCM Agreement groups subsidies as prohibited (the 'red light' category), actionable (open to countervailing duty) and non-actionable (R&D, regional and environmental).
India argues that MSP procurement for the National Food Security Act is treated as an Amber Box subsidy using an outdated historical reference price.

secs.t: Terms → meaning: MFN, AoA boxes, de minimis, tariffication, Peace Clause — Other terms

x: The de minimis limit is 5% of production value for developed countries and 10% for developing countries.
Developing countries had to cut 24% over 10 years, not 6.
The Bali Peace Clause shields developing-country public stockholding programmes from disputes until a permanent solution is found.

secs.t: WTO agreements → subject, year and India's compliance

x: TRIPS concerns minimum IPR standards, TRIMS concerns trade-related investment measures, GATS concerns services, and SPS/TBT concern health and technical standards.

India's WTO-linked laws include the Geographical Indications of Goods Act, 1999 for GI protection and the PPV&FR Act, 2001 for plant varieties and farmers' rights (both under TRIPS), and the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 for SPS/TBT food-safety standards.

secs.t: Issues and India's stand — PSH, e-commerce moratorium, fisheries Phase 2

x: MC14 did not produce a permanent solution; India and the African Group continued to seek a permanent shield for programmes such as the NFSA.
The lapse of the e-commerce moratorium exposed developing countries to the loss of tariff revenue on digital imports.
The moratorium on customs duties on electronic transmissions had existed since 1998 and lapsed for the first time on 31 March 2026.

secs.t: Dispute settlement — Appellate Body crisis and cases involving India

x: DS541 concerned India's export subsidies under the Merchandise Exports from India Scheme, SEZ and EOU schemes.
The ICT-tariff dispute was brought by
the European Union, Japan and Taiwan
and concerned duties on phones and ICT goods vis-à-vis the ITA.
The declaration sought reform of IMF and World Bank quotas and voting, along with restoration of the two-tier WTO dispute-settlement system.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: India fears that plurilateral initiatives such as the IFD and E-Commerce Agreement may fragment the WTO by weakening the consensus-based multilateral approach.

The Fisheries Subsidies Agreement is the WTO's first agreement with an environmental-sustainability objective, the moratorium lapsed for the first time since 1998, and India joined the fisheries agreement in July 2026.

rows.title: FDI and FPI policy in India - routes, sectoral caps, trends; FTAs and CEPAs signed by India
sub: Group-II M2-A-41: Foreign Direct Investment - policy, routes, sectoral caps and recent trends

secs.t: FDI vs FPI — definitions, types and classification of foreign capital

x: Foreign capital includes FDI, trade credit, NRI deposits and external commercial borrowings.
Participatory notes are offshore derivative instruments issued by registered FPIs to overseas investors who are not registered with SEBI.
ADRs and GDRs represent equity raised abroad through depository receipts and are counted as
portfolio investment
in balance of payments data.
FCCBs are debt instruments and are classified under external commercial borrowings, even though they may carry a conversion feature.

secs.t: Acts, committees, policy bodies and Press Note 3

x: DPIIT is under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, handles the nodal role for FDI policy and data, and its FIF Portal has been part of the National Single Window System since August 2022.
Press Note 3, issued in April 2020, required Government approval for FDI from land-border countries and sought to prevent opportunistic takeovers during the COVID-19 period.

From 1 May 2026, foreign firms with Chinese or Hong Kong beneficial ownership up to 10% may use the automatic route, but entities registered in China, Hong Kong or another land-border country remain excluded.

secs.t: Routes and sectoral caps → limit and route — Routes

x: Under the automatic route, no prior approval of the RBI or the Government is required.
The statement that all sectors are exclusively on the automatic route is incorrect.

secs.t: Routes and sectoral caps → limit and route — Sector caps

x: Exam angle: "Budget 2025-26 FDI limit for insurance" - 100%; "multi-brand retail cap" - 51%.
The 100% insurance FDI limit was enabled through an amendment to the
FEMA (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019

All four categories are valid: (1) 100% automatic sectors such as civil aviation MRO, ports and railway infrastructure; (2) Government-route sectors with varying caps, such as multi-brand retail, satellites, broadcasting and print media; (3) automatic up to a cap with approval beyond, such as private banks; and (4) fixed-cap-only sectors.
Budget 2025-26 raised the insurance FDI limit to 100% (automatic, subject to IRDAI), on the condition that the entire premium is invested in India.

secs.t: E-commerce FDI and prohibited sectors

x: The July 2026 relaxation allowed inventory-based e-commerce FDI where the inventory is used to export domestically manufactured goods.
Railway operations are prohibited except for permitted activities, but
railway infrastructure
is included among sectors permitting 100% automatic FDI.
Trading in TDRs, manufacture of tobacco cigars or cigarettes, prohibited railway operations, and real-estate business or farmhouses are all included in the prohibited list.

secs.t: Data — FDI flows, sources and sectors

x: Outward FDI was $23.6 billion in FY 2025, with Singapore, the United States and the UAE among the leading destinations.
The cited FY 2025-26 table gives record gross FDI of $94.6 billion and net FDI of $7.6 billion.
Net FDI peaked at
$44.0 billion in 2020-21
, before falling below $1 billion in 2024-25 and recovering to $7.6 billion in 2025-26.
According to the UNCTAD World Investment Report 2026, global FDI
rose by 6 per cent to $1.6 trillion

secs.t: Data — FPI debt limits, drivers and flows

x: FPI flows are strongly affected by US interest rates and global risk sentiment, and a flight to safety can cause outflows; domestic fundamentals are not the sole determinant.
India's inclusion in the JP Morgan Emerging Market bond index, with a target weight of 10%, is expected to draw passive bond inflows.

secs.t: Places — FDI by state and Andhra Pradesh

x: Maharashtra ranked first, Karnataka second and Tamil Nadu third during the first half of FY 2025-26.
The ascending order was Bangalore, Chennai, New Delhi and Mumbai.
Andhra Pradesh's Industrial Development Policy 4.0 targets at least $10 billion in FDI.

secs.t: Issues — weak net FDI and India's RCEP exit

x: Net FDI is reduced by profit repatriation, outward FDI by Indian firms and PE/VC exits through mechanisms such as IPOs.
India withdrew over concerns about China's market dominance, the rise in its trade deficit with China, and possible adverse effects on agriculture, dairy and small industries.
The India-China trade deficit increased from $53.5 billion in 2018–19 to $99.2 billion in 2024–25, strengthening concerns associated with joining RCEP.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Inventory e-commerce FDI for exports was associated with July 2026, PN3 relaxation with May 2026, and the UK CETA with 15 July 2026.
The debate arises because gross FDI can include accounting changes, whereas the amount of fresh capital may be considerably lower, as reflected in the difference between gross and net figures.

units.title: Financial Institutions, RBI and Monetary Policy, Banking Reforms, NPAs, Financial Markets, SEBI, Indian Tax System, GST, Centre-State Financial Relations, Public Debt and Expenditure, Fiscal Policy and Budget

rows.title: Structure of the Indian financial system - banks, NBFCs, development finance institutions, cooperatives
sub: Group-II M2-A-28: Non-banking financial companies, cooperative banks and microfinance

secs.t: Financial system — definitions, types and classification — Organised vs unorganised money market

x: Call money, Treasury bills, commercial bills and certificates of deposit
are components of the organised financial system.
Indigenous bankers and moneylenders
form part of the unorganised money market.
Money-market mutual funds and DFHI
are included in the organised money market.
The APPSC-G2 2017 key treated
finance companies
as outside the organised money market.

secs.t: Financial system — definitions, types and classification — Classification of financial institutions

x: RBI classifies
NABARD, NHB and SIDBI
as refinance institutions.
The five RBI-regulated and supervised AIFIs are
EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI and NaBFID
Under the older classification, RCTC and TFCI were specialised financial institutions.
The RBI helped set up IDBI, SIDBI, NABARD, NHB, Exim Bank and NEDB.
LIC, UTI and GIC were the
public-sector investment institutions

secs.t: Terms → meaning

x: An indigenous banker accepts deposits and lends, while combining banking activities with trade or commission business.
Shroffs, Seths, Multanis and Chettiars
are identified as indigenous bankers who accept deposits and deal in hundis.
Shadow banking is bank-like credit intermediation outside full banking regulation; NBFCs and money-market or liquid funds are examples.

secs.t: Regulators → sector

x: SEBI
regulates securities markets and FPIs; it received statutory status in 1992.
IFSCA is the unified regulator for
International Financial Services Centres, including GIFT City
, and began functioning in April 2020.
NHB
plays a quasi-regulatory role in relation to Housing Finance Companies; NABARD and SIDBI have comparable roles in other sectors.

secs.t: Development finance and other institutions → year and role, FIRSTs — DFIs - year and sector

x: Exam angle: "Establishment of which institution began the era of development financing" - IFCI.
EXIM Bank was established in January 1982, supports foreign-trade finance including lines of credit abroad, and is headquartered in Mumbai.
ICICI provided private-sector industrial credit, IDBI was the apex industrial development bank, Exim Bank financed export-import activity, and SIDBI focused on MSME finance.
The correct order is IFCI (1948), IDBI (1964), Exim Bank (1982) and SIDBI (1990).
The Government and LIC are together offloading a combined
stake in IDBI Bank to a private buyer.

secs.t: Development finance and other institutions → year and role, FIRSTs — NHB and RDCL

x: RDCL received RBI registration in January 2025, had equity participation from NHB and was created to deepen the residential mortgage-backed securities market.
NHB was established in 1988 and remained wholly RBI-owned until ownership was taken over by the Central Government in 2019.
LIC was established in 1956, UTI in 1964, GIC in 1972 and CRISIL in 1987.

secs.t: NBFCs — registration, categories and features vs banks — Registration and categories

x: An NBFC is registered under the
Companies Act
, although it is regulated by the Reserve Bank for the activities covered by the applicable regulatory framework.
The framework permits 100 per cent foreign direct investment in NBFCs through the automatic route.
The minimum net owned funds are ₹10 crore for NBFC-MFI, ₹10 crore for general NBFC-ICC and ₹20 crore for HFCs.

secs.t: NBFCs — registration, categories and features vs banks — Scale-Based Regulation (SBR)

x: The Top Layer is kept empty in normal circumstances and is intended for a sharp rise in systemic risk.
The RBI rejected Tata Sons’ bid to surrender its NBFC licence and asked it to prepare for listing.
A proposal seeks to replace the parametric scoring model with a simple ₹1 lakh crore asset-size test for identifying Upper Layer NBFCs.

secs.t: Cooperative credit structure and urban cooperative banks

x: The correct matching is State–StCB, District–DCCB, Village short-term–PACS and Village long-term–PCARDB.
UCBs traditionally faced dual control by the State Registrar of Cooperative Societies and the RBI.
Following the PMC Bank crisis, the 2020 amendment brought management, capital, audit and resolution of UCBs and multi-state cooperative banks under stronger RBI supervision.
Sahakar Sarathi was proposed as a shared-services entity for
rural cooperative banks

secs.t: Rural credit — NABARD, RRBs, SHG-Bank Linkage; persons and data

x: Commercial banks, RRBs and cooperative banks are implementing banks under the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme.
After amalgamation, there were 28 RRBs with more than 22,000 branches spread across 700 districts.
NABARD
manages RIDF (funded by banks' PSL shortfalls), refinances StCBs, RRBs and land development banks and supervises RRBs and cooperative banks.

secs.t: Acts, committees and stress episodes — NBFCs and microfinance — Acts, ordinances and committees

x: NBFC-MFIs keep at least 75% of assets in microfinance loans, the household income cap is ₹3 lakh a year and repayment is capped at 50% of income.
The Ordinance required district registration, restricted doorstep recovery and capped interest.
The committee proposed limits on lending, including no more than two MFIs per borrower; it did not support unlimited lending.

secs.t: Acts, committees and stress episodes — NBFCs and microfinance — Stress episodes

x: Defaults by
Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services Limited
(IL&FS), an infrastructure NBFC, set off a liquidity crisis in September 2018.
DHFL (2019) was the first financial services company resolved under the IBC, using the special FSP rules made under Section 227; Piramal acquired it in 2021.
The crisis involved multiple lending, over-indebtedness, coercive recovery and borrower suicides; the MFI loan book in Andhra Pradesh collapsed rather than rapidly expanding.

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh — cooperative credit data, AP Grameena Bank, cooperative laws

x: Andhra Pradesh has the apex APCOB with 18 branches, 13 DCCBs with 436 branches and 2,024 PACS.
The relevant laws are the AP Cooperative Societies Act, 1964 and the AP Mutually Aided Cooperative Societies Act, 1995.
Under Section 75 of the AP Cooperative Societies Act, 1964, the Tribunal is appellate under that Act and has original jurisdiction under the MACS Act.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Regulatory arbitrage describes the use of differences in regulatory treatment to conduct activities through less strictly regulated financial entities, a criticism associated with shadow banking.

IFCI was set up in 1948, the AP microfinance crisis came in 2010, IL&FS defaulted in September 2018, and DHFL (2019) was the first financial services company resolved under the IBC, with Piramal acquiring it in 2021.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India - establishment, organisation and functions
sub: Group-II M2-A-20: Reserve Bank of India - establishment, organisation and functions

secs.t: RBI establishment — timeline and FIRSTs

x: The correct sequence is Hilton Young Commission in 1926, RBI Act in 1934, commencement of RBI operations in 1935 and nationalisation in 1949.
Ambedkar gave evidence before the Commission in 1925, and his ideas helped shape the concept and design of the RBI.
The RBI was nationalised under the Reserve Bank of India (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948, with effect from 1 January 1949.

secs.t: Persons → role: Governors, Deputy Governors, Ambedkar

x: The four Deputy Governors comprise two from within the RBI, one commercial banker and one economist who heads monetary policy.
Sir Osborne Smith was the first Governor of the RBI from 1935 to 1937 and signed no Indian note because King Edward VIII had abdicated.
Sanjay Malhotra
has been RBI Governor since December 2024 and chairs the MPC and the Payments Regulatory Board.

secs.t: Organisation and places — board, offices, institutes, presses, mints

x: Exam angle: "Bank Note Press is located at" - Dewas.
The RBI’s headquarters is in Mumbai, it has offices at 31 locations, and it is popularly associated with the nickname ‘Mint Street’.
The local boards are located in New Delhi, Chennai, Kolkata and Mumbai for the North, South, East and West regions respectively.
The Currency Note Press is at Nashik, the Bank Note Press is at Dewas, and RBI-owned BRBNMPL presses are located at Mysuru and Salboni.

secs.t: Functions of RBI — and what RBI does not do

x: The MPC is a six-member statutory body under the RBI Act and sets the policy repo rate as part of the monetary policy framework.
Section 22
of the RBI Act confers the sole right to issue banknotes on the RBI, except for the one-rupee note.

The RBI’s government-banking function is based on Section 20 for the Centre and Sections 21 and 21A for States, and includes receipts, payments, public debt management, Ways and Means Advances and overdrafts.
The Public Debt Management Cell was created to ease the potential conflict between public debt management and the conduct of monetary policy.

secs.t: Currency management — issuer, reserve systems, denominations, note features — Issuing authority

x: Currency notes are liabilities of the RBI and are backed by assets including gold, foreign securities and Government securities held in the Issue Department.
The Governor signs RBI notes, the one-rupee note is signed by the Finance Secretary, and the RBI distributes coins on behalf of the Government of India.
Under the earlier Proportional Reserve System, two-fifths of the backing had to be in gold or sterling, with gold valued at not less than ₹40 crore.

secs.t: Currency management — issuer, reserve systems, denominations, note features — Denominations and demonetisation

x: The ₹10,000 note was introduced in 1938, demonetised in 1946, reintroduced in 1954 and demonetised again in 1978.
Indian currency notes carry 17 languages in total: Hindi and English on the front and 15 scheduled languages in the language panel on the back.
MANI (Mobile Aided Note Identifier) is an RBI app (2020) that helps visually impaired users identify note denominations.

secs.t: Acts and Sections → provision; RBI autonomy — Legal basis of regulation

x: The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 covers licensing, branch opening, management, amalgamation, cash reserve and liquidity requirements, audit and inspection.
Under Section 26A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, unclaimed deposits of ten or more years are transferred to the DEA Fund, but the depositor’s right to claim survives.
Section 7 permits the Central Government to issue directions in the public interest after consultation with
the RBI Governor

secs.t: Acts and Sections → provision; RBI autonomy — Licensing, branches, mergers

x: Banks, SFBs, payments banks, LABs and RRBs may open branches without prior approval provided 25% of new branches are in unbanked rural areas.
RB-IOS 2026 covers banks, RRBs, UCBs, NBFCs and non-bank payment operators.
The MPC framework and inflation-targeting law introduced in 2016 gave the RBI operational independence on policy rates.

secs.t: Boards, committees, ombudsman and surplus transfer — Boards and committees

x: The Payments Regulatory Board replaced the BPSS in
October 2025
, while its first meeting was held in January 2026.
RB-IOS 2026 follows the principle of “
One Nation, One Ombudsman
” and covers banks, RRBs, UCBs, NBFCs and payment operators.
The framework distinguished realised equity from revaluation balances and provided for a Contingent Risk Buffer.

secs.t: Boards, committees, ombudsman and surplus transfer — Income and surplus transfer

x: RBI income includes interest on securities and loans, foreign exchange gains and fees.
The RBI recorded a surplus of
₹2.86 lakh crore
for 2025–26, described as its highest-ever surplus.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Special FCNR(B) inflows contributed to surplus liquidity, prompting the RBI to absorb funds through VRRR operations.
RBI independence and the transfer of its surplus are important elements of fiscal-monetary coordination.
The repo rate was kept unchanged at
in August 2026.

rows.title: Money supply - M0 to M4, high-powered money, money multiplier, velocity
sub: Group-II M2-A-19: Functions of money; measures of money supply (M1 to M4) and high-powered money

secs.t: Money — functions and kinds

x: Medium of exchange is a primary function, store of value is a secondary function and basis of credit is a contingent function.
The contingent functions include acting as a basis of credit, distribution of national income and
giving liquidity
Not
every highly liquid financial asset is legal tender
; near money such as time deposits and Treasury bills cannot directly settle ordinary payments.

secs.t: Terms → meaning

x: Exam angle: "Seigniorage refers to" - profit earned by the central bank/government by issuing currency.
Time deposits are highly liquid assets but cannot directly be used to pay for goods and services, making them near money.
Velocity tends to be higher among low-income spenders and during booms, when money changes hands more frequently.

secs.t: Indian currency history — Acts and FIRSTs

x: Bank of Hindostan operated from 1770 to 1832, the General Bank of Bengal and Bihar was established in 1773, and the Controller of Currency transferred note issue to RBI in 1935.
The
Paper Currency Act, 1861
, gave the Government the monopoly of note issue, replacing the earlier private and presidency-bank pattern of issuance.

secs.t: Monetary aggregates — M0 (high-powered money) to M4, NM0-NM3, L1-L3 — High-powered money (M0)

x: Other deposits with RBI include deposits of quasi-government and financial institutions, including primary dealers, foreign central banks and governments, and international agencies such as the IMF.
The uses-side composition of high-powered money includes currency held by the public, banks' cash in hand, banks' deposits with RBI and other deposits with RBI.

secs.t: Monetary aggregates — M0 (high-powered money) to M4, NM0-NM3, L1-L3 — M1 to M4 (Second Working Group, 1977)

x: Exam angle: "which is the broadest/most liquid", and matching aggregates with components.
M2 equals M1 plus post office savings bank deposits; M3 equals M1 plus time deposits with the banking system; and M4 includes all post office deposits except NSCs.
The monetary aggregate framework from M1 to M4 was introduced on the recommendation of the
Second Working Group on Money Supply

secs.t: Monetary aggregates — M0 (high-powered money) to M4, NM0-NM3, L1-L3 — New monetary and liquidity aggregates (1998)

x: The 1998 group was the third working group; the Second Working Group (1977) gave M1-M4.
NM0–NM3 are residency-based aggregates that distinguish short-term from long-term deposits.

secs.t: Money multiplier and credit creation — formula, policy effects

x: A rising money multiplier indicates that the banking system is converting reserve money into a larger volume of deposits and credit, reflecting
better financial intermediation
The RBI creates reserve money through the issue of notes, while commercial banks create deposit money by lending beyond the reserves they are required to hold under CRR and SLR rules.

secs.t: Economists → theories of demand for money

x: Under Keynesian liquidity preference, speculative demand for money varies inversely with the rate of interest.
Baumol-Tobin analysis treats cash holding as involving an opportunity cost, making transaction demand interest-sensitive.
Irving Fisher is associated with the quantity theory, Marshall and Pigou with the Cambridge cash-balance approach, Keynes with liquidity preference, and Friedman with the modern quantity theory.

secs.t: Data — multiplier, currency in circulation, e-Rupee

x: The CRR was reduced by 100 basis points to
3.0 per cent
of NDTL, releasing approximately ₹2.5 lakh crore by December 2025.
The subsequent rise in currency in circulation indicates that demonetisation did not permanently reduce cash use.
Offline payments, programmability for DBT and a cross-border pilot with the UAE are identified features or uses.

secs.t: Demonetisation episodes and counterfeit currency (FICN)

x: The High Denomination Bank Notes (Demonetisation) Act, 1978, under Morarji Desai, demonetised the
notes to curb black money.
The 2016 announcement withdrew
notes, effective from midnight.
The legal basis was
Section 26(2) of the RBI Act, 1934
, on the recommendation of the RBI’s Central Board.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The reported criticism is that demonetisation's black-money gains remain unproven, while cash use and fake notes continue to persist.
All three developments were reported: the CRR was cut to 3%, the multiplier rose to 6.21, and fake currency continued to be seized ten years after demonetisation.
NCRB's Crime in India 2024 recorded seizure of ₹54.61 crore in fake currency, including about six lakh ₹500 notes and over one lakh ₹2,000 notes.

rows.title: Monetary policy - objectives, instruments (CRR, SLR, repo, reverse repo, MSF, OMO, LAF), transmission
sub: Group-II M2-A-22: Instruments of monetary policy and control of credit - quantitative and qualitative
Group-II M2-A-23: Monetary policy transmission - problems and effectiveness in India

secs.t: Monetary policy — authority, objectives and framework phases

x: Post-1991 reforms progressively deregulated interest rates, reducing direct administrative determination and allowing greater market and bank influence.
Governor
Shaktikanta Das
traced these phases in “Seven Ages of India's Monetary Policy” on 24 January 2020 at St. Stephen's College.
The framework was considered opaque because markets could not predict the RBI's actions when growth, inflation, exchange-rate and credit indicators conflicted.

secs.t: Instruments — quantitative vs qualitative, main instrument

x: Variable reserve ratio
, including CRR and SLR, is a quantitative or general credit-control instrument.
The MPC sets the policy repo rate to achieve the inflation target, while liquidity operations help keep money-market rates close to that rate.
Under FIT, the repo rate functions as the single operating policy rate and is the most closely watched signal of monetary policy.

secs.t: Terms → meaning: policy rates, LAF corridor, stance — Policy rates

x: The current MSF rate is repo plus 25 basis points, and banks may dip into SLR holdings up to 2% of NDTL.
The bank rate is associated with rediscounting bills and longer-term lending and is aligned with the MSF; the repo rate is the policy rate for overnight collateralised lending.
The fixed-rate reverse repo absorbs funds against Government securities and is now used at the RBI's discretion, while the SDF absorbs funds without collateral.
The repo rate declined by 125 basis points from 6.50% in February 2025 to 5.25%.

secs.t: Terms → meaning: policy rates, LAF corridor, stance — MSF and the corridor

x: Exam angle: order of the corridor - SDF (floor) < repo < MSF = bank rate (ceiling).
A hawkish stance worries about inflation and tightens; worry about growth with an easing bias is dovish.
The stance moved from neutral to accommodative in April 2025, returned to neutral in June 2025 and remained neutral through August 2026.

secs.t: CRR and SLR — features, legal basis, floor and ceiling

x: SLR may be maintained by banks themselves in cash, gold, unencumbered government securities including Treasury Bills and State Development Loans, and other approved securities.
The SLR range is 0-40% of NDTL, and the 25% floor was removed by the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2007.
The required reserve ratio is the CRR: the share of NDTL banks must keep as a cash balance with the RBI (Sec 42, RBI Act), earning no interest.

secs.t: Tool → effect: money supply, demand, transmission channels, bond yields — Dear money vs cheap money

x: A contractionary policy raises CRR, SLR and policy rates and sells Government securities through OMO, thereby reducing liquidity and demand.
A CRR or SLR cut releases funds for lending and raises the money multiplier, subject to the banking system's willingness and ability to lend.
Raising CRR withdraws lendable funds, reducing money circulation and demand.

secs.t: Tool → effect: money supply, demand, transmission channels, bond yields — Transmission channels

x: Indian G-sec yields are influenced by all three factors: US Federal Reserve actions, RBI actions, and domestic inflation and short-term interest rates.
The OMO purchases of ₹1 lakh crore were intended to
stabilise bond yields
and support orderly financial-market conditions.
S&P raised India from
BBB- to BBB
in 2025-26, which helped narrow the sovereign spread and lower borrowing costs.

secs.t: Liquidity management and sterilisation — LAF, SDF, VRR/VRRR, I-CRR, MSS — Short-term windows

x: LAF is the primary framework through which the RBI injects liquidity through repo and absorbs liquidity through reverse repo and SDF operations on a day-to-day basis.
VRR injects liquidity, while VRRR absorbs surplus liquidity for longer maturities than the overnight SDF.
Fine-tuning operations, generally involving short-term VRR or VRRR auctions, are conducted to align liquidity conditions with the prevailing monetary policy stance.

secs.t: Liquidity management and sterilisation — LAF, SDF, VRR/VRRR, I-CRR, MSS — Durable liquidity and reserve tools

x: Under the MSS, introduced in April 2004, the RBI issues Treasury Bills and securities to absorb rupees created by foreign-exchange purchases.
When foreign-exchange inflows increase rupee liquidity, the RBI may sell government securities or conduct liquidity-absorption operations to offset the impact.
The RBI may sell government securities through OMO or MSS and conduct VRRR operations to absorb excess liquidity.

secs.t: Liquidity management and sterilisation — LAF, SDF, VRR/VRRR, I-CRR, MSS — Liquidity conditions - surplus vs deficit

x: Surplus liquidity can lower market rates below the repo rate and facilitate transmission.

secs.t: Lending rate benchmarks — who sets which rate, committees and directions — Who sets which rate

x: CRR and SLR are RBI-set requirements, MCLR is computed internally by each bank, and the call money rate is market-determined.

secs.t: Lending rate benchmarks — who sets which rate, committees and directions — Benchmark evolution

x: From 1 October 2019, such loans had to be linked to an external benchmark, including the repo rate, the three- or six-month Treasury-bill yield, or an FBIL-published rate.
EBLR links lending rates directly to an external benchmark such as the repo rate, allowing loans to reprice more quickly than Base Rate or MCLR loans.
MCLR incorporates marginal deposit cost, CRR/SLR carry, operating cost and tenor premium.

secs.t: Lending rate benchmarks — who sets which rate, committees and directions — Committee and directions

x: The proposed directions retain external-benchmark linkage for floating-rate personal and MSME loans and provide for interest on the
daily reducing balance
The RBI’s Internal Study Group on the working of the MCLR system was chaired by
Janak Raj
The study group found weak MCLR transmission, recommended external benchmarking, and its recommendations led to the EBLR mandate effective from 1 October 2019.

secs.t: Data — policy rates then and now, pass-through

x: The Economic Survey 2025-26 reported that WALR on fresh rupee loans fell by
64 basis points
in FY26, which it called robust pass-through.
The August 2026 levels were repo 5.25 per cent, SDF 5.00 per cent, MSF 5.50 per cent and CRR 3 per cent.
The CRR declined by 1 percentage point, which is equal to
100 basis points

secs.t: Issues — challenges after 1991, monetary vs fiscal policy, obstacles to transmission — Challenges after 1991

x: The system of automatic monetisation through ad hoc Treasury Bills ended in 1997 and was replaced by
Ways and Means Advances
Oil prices, global rate cycles and wars are external shocks that can affect inflation, capital flows and exchange rates.
Large government borrowing, and earlier automatic monetisation through ad hoc Treasury Bills, could increase money supply and inflation, producing fiscal dominance.

secs.t: Issues — challenges after 1991, monetary vs fiscal policy, obstacles to transmission — Monetary vs fiscal policy - complementary roles against inflation

x: Supply-driven food and fuel inflation may require
buffer stocks, duty cuts and farm reforms
, whereas CRR, SLR and policy rates primarily influence aggregate demand.
The government, Finance Ministry and Parliament conduct fiscal policy through spending, taxes, subsidies and borrowing.
Fiscal policy can face legislative and implementation lags.

secs.t: Issues — challenges after 1991, monetary vs fiscal policy, obstacles to transmission — Obstacles to transmission

x: All four conditions can obstruct transmission by keeping funding costs or market yields high, limiting repricing, or placing credit activity outside the formal monetary-policy channel.
NPAs and weak balance sheets can weaken transmission.
Heavy government borrowing is an obstacle because it keeps yields high (crowding out).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Weak pass-through to deposit rates, the movement of large firms towards non-bank credit, and the RBI’s limited influence over food inflation are all identified concerns.
The Draft Interest Rate Directions, 2026 aim to improve monetary-policy transmission and prevent excessive pricing for small borrowers.
Since the repo rate operates mainly through demand and financial conditions, it cannot directly correct disruptions originating on the food or fuel supply side.

rows.title: Monetary Policy Committee and the flexible inflation targeting framework
sub: Group-II M2-A-21: Monetary policy - objectives, framework, MPC and inflation targeting

secs.t: Framework — objectives and phases from monetary targeting (1985) to FIT (2016)

x: Monetary targeting prevailed during 1985–1998, followed by the multiple-indicator approach during 1998–2014, the glide path during 2014–2016, and flexible inflation targeting from 2016 onwards.
Price stability is the primary objective, with growth kept in mind.
Maximising Government revenue
is not an objective of monetary policy.

secs.t: Committees → recommendation

x: The
Sukhamoy Chakravarty Committee
, constituted in 1985, recommended monetary targeting with feedback and dealt with the organised money market.
N. Vaghul headed the 1987 committee that prepared a blueprint for the money market and contributed to the introduction of Commercial Paper in 1990.
The Urjit Patel Committee recommended dropping the multiple-indicator approach, adopting CPI as the nominal anchor and establishing an MPC-based rate-setting framework.

secs.t: Acts, agreements and Sections → provision

x: Exam angle: "In which year was the RBI Act amended for FIT?" The answer is
The 2016 amendment inserted
Sections 45Z to 45ZO
into the RBI Act, 1934, providing the statutory framework for the MPC and inflation-targeting provisions.
Failure is defined as average CPI inflation remaining
above 6 per cent or below 2 per cent for three consecutive quarters

secs.t: Data — inflation target periods and CPI anchor

x: The August 2016 notification covered the period up to 31 March 2021; the March 2021 notification covered April 2021–March 2026; and the 25 March 2026 notification covers April 2026–March 2031.
The 25 March 2026 notification retained the 4 per cent CPI target with a 2 percentage point tolerance band for 2026–2031.
CPI-Combined is compiled by the NSO under MoSPI, and the new series released on 12 Feb 2026 has base year 2024 (the earlier base was 2012).

secs.t: Monetary Policy Committee — basis, composition, voting, quorum

x: The law requires at least four meetings a year; meeting bi-monthly (six times) is only the practice.
The three external members are appointed by the Central Government for
four years and are not eligible for reappointment
The MPC fixes the policy repo rate required to achieve the notified inflation target, and its decisions bind the RBI.

secs.t: Policy stances and the MPC decision record, 2022–2026

x: The MPC held the repo rate at 5.25 per cent in February, June and August 2026, and the decisions were unanimous with a neutral stance.
Withdrawal of accommodation is a tightening bias that drains excess liquidity.
Under a neutral stance, the central bank retains the flexibility to raise or reduce rates according to economic and inflation data.

secs.t: Issues — global monetary tightening and spillovers to India

x: Global monetary tightening can encourage capital outflows from India, put pressure on the rupee and raise imported inflation through exchange-rate and import-cost channels.
In June 2026, the MPC retained the repo rate at 5.25 per cent but reduced its FY27 growth forecast despite global tightening concerns.
The inflation forecast assumed crude oil at
95 dollars per barrel
, partly reflecting risks arising from the West Asia conflict.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The failure clause was first invoked in 2022.
Both the Assertion and Reason are true.
Food and supply shocks are outside the MPC's direct control; this is one reason for the criticism of headline targeting.
Andhra Pradesh’s CPI inflation was 4.9%, above the national rate of 3.9% mentioned for the comparison.

rows.title: Banking in India - nationalisation, structure, priority sector, small finance and payments banks
sub: Group-II M2-A-24: Indian banking - structure, nationalisation and phases of development

secs.t: Banking — definitions, types and FIRSTs — FIRSTs

x: The first Presidency bank was set up in 1806 as the
Bank of Calcutta
(also called the Presidency Bank of Bengal) and was later renamed the Bank of Bengal.
HSBC
introduced the first ATM in India in Mumbai in 1987.
Punjab National Bank
is described as the first bank with wholly Indian capital and management.
UTI Bank was the first private bank established after the 1994 liberalisation of banking.

secs.t: Banking — definitions, types and FIRSTs — Organised vs unorganised

x: The associate banks of SBI and Bharatiya Mahila Bank were merged into SBI with effect from
1 April 2017
NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits or issue cheques, and their deposits are not covered by DICGC insurance.
DICGC was formed in 1978 through the merger of the Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Credit Guarantee Corporation of India.

secs.t: Banks → founders, headquarters, year

x: Dr Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramayya founded Andhra Insurance Company, Bharat Lakshmi Bank and the Krishna District Co-operative Bank.
Allahabad Bank dates from 1865 and merged into Indian Bank, while Canara Bank was founded by Ammembal Subba Rao Pai and took over Syndicate Bank.
Dr Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramayya founded Andhra Bank (20 Nov 1923, Machilipatnam), and it merged into Union Bank of India in 2020.

secs.t: Bank nationalisation — Acts, dates and rounds

x: The correct sequence is RBI nationalisation in 1949, SBI formation in 1955, nationalisation of 14 banks in 1969 and nationalisation of six banks in 1980.
Nationalisation sought to reduce the control of industrial houses and remedy the neglect of agriculture and small units; it did not aim to preserve exclusive control by them.
Bank nationalisation was associated with expansion of branches and increased lending to priority sectors, including agriculture and small units.
Indira Gandhi set out the intent behind bank nationalisation in a note titled “
Stray Thoughts on Bank Nationalisation

secs.t: Committees and Acts → small finance banks, payments banks and RRBs

x: The Nachiket Mor Committee was constituted in 2013, and both categories arose from niche licences; commercial banks are now licensed on tap.
Payments banks are licensed under
Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
and are public limited companies under the Companies Act, 2013.
Regional Rural Banks were initially created through an ordinance and were subsequently governed by the
Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976

secs.t: Committees and Acts → small finance banks, payments banks and RRBs — SFB vs payments bank

x: Small Finance Banks can lend and must allocate 75% of ANBC to PSL, while Payments Banks accept only demand deposits and cannot lend.
Payments Banks are required to invest 75% of demand deposits in SLR government securities or Treasury Bills with maturity up to one year.
The minimum capital specified for Small Finance Banks is
₹100 crore
, while Payments Banks require ₹100 crore of paid-up voting equity capital.

secs.t: Committees and Acts → small finance banks, payments banks and RRBs — Regional Rural Banks — features

x: An RRB has a 50:15:35 shareholding pattern among the Central Government, State Government and sponsor bank, respectively.
Fifteen RRBs were amalgamated with effect from 1 May 2025 under the One State-One RRB initiative, leaving 28 RRBs thereafter.
The four merged RRBs were Andhra Pragathi, AP Grameena Vikas, Chaitanya Godavari and Saptagiri.

secs.t: Lead Bank Scheme and SLBC — features

x: Under the Service Area Approach, each rural bank branch plans credit for a specified set of villages.
District-level forums under the Lead Bank Scheme are conducted by
the Lead District Manager
Union Bank of India
acts as the Lead Bank and the convener of the State Level Bankers’ Committee in Andhra Pradesh.
The Lead Bank Scheme began in 1969, the same year 14 banks were nationalised.

secs.t: Terms → meaning: banking operations and customer rules

x: Para-banking refers to services beyond the traditional acceptance of deposits and provision of loans, including credit cards, insurance, factoring and mutual fund distribution.
From
1 October 2021
, a penalty of ₹10,000 per ATM applies when an ATM remains out of cash for more than 10 hours in a month.
Banks can use Aadhaar for KYC verification with the customer's consent (APPSC-GS 2019).

secs.t: Data — bank counts, outreach, AP deposits, credit and RRB performance

x: The ratio declined from 162% to 157.40%, but remained substantially above the RBI norm of 60%.
1.81 lakh branches, 17.36 lakh business correspondents, 99.92% village coverage within 5 km and 58.77 crore PMJDY accounts.
Aggregate deposits increased from ₹5,32,801 crore in December 2024 to ₹6,08,834 crore in December 2025.
Bank credit in Andhra Pradesh stood at
in December 2025; the December 2024 figure was ₹8,61,580 crore.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The United Forum of Bank Unions held a strike on 12 September 2026 seeking a five-day week in public sector banks.
The banking-sector significance highlighted is the 4R strategy for public sector banks and GNPA of 2.2% in September 2025, a multi-decadal low.
In August 2026 the RBI resumed on-tap licences for
Urban Co-operative Banks
(UCBs).

rows.title: Banking sector reforms - Narasimham Committee I and II, Basel norms, bank mergers, privatisation debate
sub: Group-II M2-A-25: Banking sector reforms - Narasimham Committees, Basel norms, consolidation and privatisation debate

secs.t: Financial sector reforms after 1991 — features

x: Post-1991 reforms introduced prudential norms for income recognition, asset classification and provisioning, along with CRAR in 1992.
SEBI received statutory status in 1992, the Banking Ombudsman was introduced in 1995, and ARCs and DRTs were associated with recovery mechanisms.
The RBI became the primary regulator, ending dual control with the Finance Ministry’s Banking Division.

secs.t: Narasimham Committees I and II → year, title, recommendations

x: The
Narasimham-I Committee
of 1991 examined the banking and financial system, including capital adequacy, prudential norms and lower SLR and CRR.
Narasimham-II focused on
bank consolidation, non-performing assets and universal banking
Narasimham-I focused on foundational banking reforms, while Narasimham-II emphasised consolidation, a three-tier structure and resolution of weak banks.
The proposed structure consisted of two or three international banks, eight to ten national banks and many local banks.

secs.t: Other committees → chair, year, subject — Committees

x: The Raghuram Rajan Committee’s report was titled “
A Hundred Small Steps
The S.H. Khan Working Group examined how the roles of banks and Development Finance Institutions could be harmonised, leading towards universal banking.
The Committee on Financial Sector Assessment, functioning during 2006–09, conducted a joint Government of India–RBI self-assessment of financial-sector stability and standards.
Goiporia dealt with customer service, Malhotra with insurance reform, C. Rangarajan with financial inclusion, and P.J. Nayak with bank-board governance.
The Nachiket Mor Committee, constituted in 2013, examined differentiated banks, including
small finance banks and payments banks

secs.t: Other committees → chair, year, subject — P.J. Nayak Committee and Banks Board Bureau

x: The Banks Board Bureau originated from the
Indradhanush
initiative and began functioning in 2016.
The
Financial Services Institutions Bureau
(FSIB) replaced the Banks Board Bureau in 2022.

secs.t: Basel Accords — bodies, years and FIRSTs

x: The Basel Accords are formulated by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), which functions under the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).
Basel II rests on three pillars:
minimum capital requirements, supervisory review and market discipline
The five fixed risk-weight buckets are associated with Basel I. Basel III introduced stronger CET1 requirements, buffers, leverage and liquidity standards.

secs.t: Data — capital adequacy norms, RBI vs BCBS

x: The BCBS minimums are CET1 4.5 per cent, Tier 1 capital 6 per cent, CCB 2.5 per cent and countercyclical buffer 0–2.5 per cent.
The comparative framework lists both the LCR and NSFR minimums at 100 per cent for BCBS and RBI norms.
In October 2025, the RBI proposed lower Basel III risk weights for
MSMEs and real estate

secs.t: Terms → meaning: capital, buffers and liquidity ratios

x: Exam angle: match each ratio to its purpose (LCR = 30 days, NSFR = 1 year, CCyB = credit boom); RBI vs BCBS minimums.
The
Liquidity Coverage Ratio
(LCR) requires a stock of high-quality liquid assets sufficient to survive a 30-day stress period.
The capital conservation buffer is 2.5 per cent over the minimum; the leverage ratio caps exposure against Tier 1 capital; LTV caps relate loans to collateral; risk weights can cool risky lending.

secs.t: Schemes → PSB recapitalisation and power-sector reform

x: The seven components were Appointments, Banks Board Bureau, Capitalisation, De-stressing, Empowerment, Framework of accountability and Governance.
Under the mechanism, the Government issues bonds to public sector banks and puts the money back into them as equity; therefore, no equivalent fresh cash leaves the budget immediately.
The record combined net profit of ₹1.98 lakh crore in FY26 was cited as meaning that budgetary recapitalisation is not currently needed.

secs.t: EASE (Enhanced Access and Service Excellence) — Reforms Agenda and Index

x: Exam angle: APPSC G1 2024 - the statement that EASE is "governed by a board of heads of premier FIs" is
false
; IBA's steering committee runs it.
Quarterly benchmarking of mid-size and large public sector banks against reform themes provides the basis for ranking them in the EASE Index.
EASE aims include financial stability, credit growth, NPA management, risk mitigation, digital transformation, customer service and inclusion.

secs.t: Bank mergers and RRB consolidation — anchor bank, year — PSB mergers

x: The mergers took effect in the order: SBI-related merger in 2017, Dena–Vijaya with Bank of Baroda in 2019, and Andhra–Corporation and Allahabad Bank mergers in 2020.
The expected gains included scale, lower costs, global-size lenders, better capital use and improved risk management.
Narasimham-II recommended consolidation through mergers of strong banks and the creation of fewer, stronger banking institutions.

secs.t: Bank mergers and RRB consolidation — anchor bank, year — RRB consolidation

x: There were originally 196 RRBs, and their number came down to 43 after the 2020–21 consolidation.
15 RRBs were amalgamated, the arrangement took effect on 1 May 2025, and the Centre retains a 50 per cent share.
Viability Plan 2.0 covers all 28 RRBs, rests on four pillars and tracks 30 parameters.

secs.t: Acts and institutions — DICGC, Banking Laws (Amendment) Act 2025

x: The deposit insurance limit was raised from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh in the
Budget, following the PMC Bank crisis.
The Act came into force on 1 August 2025 and made 19 amendments across the RBI Act, Banking Regulation Act, SBI Act, and the Banking Companies Acts of 1970 and 1980.

secs.t: Privatisation debate — issues

x: Following LIC’s acquisition of a majority stake in 2019, RBI reclassified IDBI Bank as a private sector lender.
Minority stake sales were considered in UCO Bank, Bank of Maharashtra, Central Bank of India, Punjab & Sind Bank and Indian Overseas Bank.
The debate balances possible gains in efficiency and governance against the social mandate of public sector banks, including rural branches and priority lending.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Budget 2026–27 announced the High Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat and restructuring of PFC and REC.
Bank mergers can involve significant
integration costs
, including the task of combining systems, personnel and operations.
The expected credit loss shift was estimated to reduce Tier-1 ratios by about
100–150 basis points
